175304: Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children. They often tried to lure people to the water in order to be baptised. In this way people sometimes drowned.
175305: A man travelling with his horse suddenly could go no further and said to a woman standing there: "What on earth is wrong with my horse?" The witch replied: "There's nothing at all wrong with that horse!" The witch stamped on the ground and then the horse went on again. The witch had made the horse stand still.
175308: A woman from Boorsem who had many children was often visited by a certain Lies who came peddling. Whenever Lies wanted to touch the children, the mother said: "Do not do to others what you would not have done to you". When one day Lies reached out her hand towards Jeanke, the mother said the same again. At that Lies became very angry.
175310: Some men who were manuring the field with four horses took a break to drink coffee. At that moment a Walloon beggar woman knocked and asked for a slice of bread. After she had been given her bread, the woman rubbed one of the horses and then left. When the men started working again, they saw that this one horse was completely covered in lice. It was so bad that they even had to take the animal to the vet.
175332: A boy from Nieuwerkerken went to play cards in Melveren until midnight or half past twelve. Every time the boy got outside the village, he was jumped by a dog that made itself carried as far as Nieuwerkerken. If the boy was accompanied home by his friends, the dog did not appear. One Saturday evening the boy managed to hit the werewolf on the head with a piece of iron. On Sunday the boy saw a man in church with a wound on his head.
175345: A hunter saw a fine hare every day. The man had often tried to shoot the hare, but he never succeeded.
175347: A man coming back from the fair around midnight walked past the chapel in the Lochtstraat. At that moment the man heard a good fifty or sixty cats miaowing. A little further on the man saw a little black cat that kept jumping up at him. After the man had kicked at the cat, the animal even jumped onto his head.
175361: Some gentlemen had asked Our Lady to free a number of Turkish slaves in the Holy Land. Later the chains of those slaves lay by the statue of Mary.
175366: Mie H. and Rik were coming back from the fair in Bocholt at night. On the way the pair were followed closely by a cat. Luckily the pair met Rik's father and Door S., who had his dog with him. Contrary to everyone's expectation, the cat was not at all afraid of the dog. Then Door took a stick and hit the cat as hard as he could. Despite the tremendous blow the cat was still not dead and ran off miaowing.
175371: Jona V.D.H. always handed out sugar lumps to the children. But whoever ate the sugar became seriously ill.
175380: Witches could effortlessly break up the relationship between two lovers or an engaged couple by means of a pin. In the same way a witch could also bring the worst enemies together.
175397: Two people from Membruggen had gone to fetch the midwife. At the white chapel in Millen they could not get through because a white woman blocked their way. The midwife, who was afraid of nothing, said: "If you are of the devil, break. If you are of God, speak!" The next moment the white woman had vanished.
175400: Will-o'-the-wisps were ghosts that often appeared in the linden tree.
175404: Some people walking home in the evening suddenly no longer dared to go on when they saw a dog with bells coming towards them. It was a werewolf.
175405: Near the Geuzentempel (Protestant church) in Alken a ghost wandered about with heavy chains on its hands and feet.
175410: On his deathbed the drossaard (bailiff) asked the priest: "Will I ever find rest?", to which the clergyman replied: "You may rest on a needle used for sewing on Sunday." Since then, whenever a woman picked up a needle on a Sunday, people said: "On a needle used for sewing on Sunday sits the drossaard of 't Hoebes."
175422: Two men went to fetch wood in Houthalen. When one of them pulled some wood from a stack, suddenly the cackling of a hundred thousand hens was heard. The other man ran away in fear. A moment later three loud bangs sounded in the house. After that all was quiet.
175425: A bachelor from Gingelom who had always been happy believed he was bewitched because he had been feeling depressed lately. In the man's pillow a rat was found that did not yet have one leg. If the rat had been complete, the man would have died. The pillow and the rat were burned.
175431: A soldier came to a house where an emaciated little child lay in bed. "Doesn't a woman come here?" asked the soldier, and they said yes. "Have that woman come, and make sure there is enough wood and peat in the house so that you can build a big fire. I'll make sure that woman leaves your child alone". The soldier stood behind the door and grabbed the witch from behind. Although the witch would not admit her guilt, the soldier kept saying: "You are tormenting that child", while pushing her closer and closer to the fire. When the witch's clothes caught fire, she said: "Take that stone out of the fire". Under the stone lay a little doll stuck full of pins.
175440: Witches mostly harmed children. They gave the children a sweet or touched them saying: "Oh, dear child!" After that the child fell ill.
175445: Parish priest V. from Neerrepen warned people about the evil done by witches. In Vliermaal a witch had taken a newborn child. The next day the child was found dead.
175456: In Hougreye there was a haunted castle. Strange noises were always heard in the attic.
175465: A man was digging near the witches' lane between eleven and twelve at night. Suddenly he saw something appear that said: "Get out of here!" But the man bravely kept working. Around midnight he again heard a shout: "Get out of here!" But there was nothing to be seen.
175479: A man often heard a strange rustling in the air. People believed it was witches flying through the air.
175480: Dorplein was haunted. Strange ghost lights were often seen there, dancing in a circle and frightening people.
175485: One day a woman from Kevelaar was walking to the station of Opoeteren. On the way she suddenly saw two will-o'-the-wisps playing with each other. When the woman had overcome her fear, she called out to the lights: "If you come from God, come closer. If you come from the devil, go away." The will-o'-the-wisps vanished at once.
175490: When someone had died, people would say: "He will come back to haunt to put his boundary post back".
175502: A man from Kuringen wanted to go to the heksenman (witch doctor). The man had to turn back because on the way he suddenly found himself before a great body of water. When the man did reach the heksenman three days later, the latter said: "Three days ago you wanted to come as well, but it didn't work then."
175506: A woman who had done bad business at the market in Weert was walking home, muttering. Suddenly she heard a voice that said: "Remorse comes after sin". The woman looked around and saw nothing but a cat.
175507: A boy made mice in the church after he had tied a knot in his handkerchief. After the priest had read prayers over the boy, he could no longer make mice.
175510: One evening the people of Horpmaal heard witches singing, but they saw nothing. The priest was on his way to a dying man to give him the last rites. When the priest walked beneath the hovering witches, the incense touched one of them. Because of this the witch fell from the sky and took on her human form again.
175515: A man coming home at night saw a small black kitten and said: "What a pretty kitten!" The animal replied: "Look, Bert says I'm a pretty kitten!"
175518: The kaartridder (card knight) of Heppeneert played a game of cards with the devil, who was recognised by his goat's legs.
175525: A dog used to haunt the churchyard. The organist got epilepsy from it.
175533: A man who went to fetch his flour from the mill in the evening met a white cat on the way. He did not dare do anything to the animal, for he knew it was better to leave alone anything that roamed about at night.
175539: Someone who had promised to make a novena died before he had been able to keep his promise. A man who went to fetch brushwood saw someone appear on a brushwood stack, who said, "I cannot be released from purgatory as long as nobody has made that novena."
175548: Because Jef S. had had a headache for quite a while, he went to a doctor. But the doctor could not help him. A woman who came peddling thought that Jef's headache might be caused by the evil hand. So Jef went to a clergyman, who advised him to stay away from his fiancée for a while. After that Jef had no more headaches. Because Jef had found out in this way that his fiancée was a witch, he broke off the engagement.
175549: Ghosts always made noise in the attic.
175572: The witches often held gatherings on the Heksenberg, where there was wild dancing. One day a man coming back from Bilzen saw the witches dancing. The witches wanted the man to drink, but he refused. After a while the man let himself be persuaded after all and said: "If there's no other way, in God's name". The next moment the man stood with the cup in his hand and all the witches had vanished. A day later the man was visited by a gentleman and a lady from Holland, who came to ask for the cup back.
175575: A witch used to live in Vliermaal. A group of men stood waiting by the witch's house to beat her to death as soon as she came out. But the witch crept outside in the shape of a cat and a few hours later slipped back in through the henhouse.
175578: A woman had made soup on a Saturday. She kept the soup in the cellar until Sunday. When the woman went to fetch the soup on Sunday, she found a toad in it. People believed the neighbour woman had conjured the toad into the soup. Witches could also infest people with lice.
175589: In the evening people were followed by a ghost in the shape of a bear.
175592: A woman from Rutten died before she had gone on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel as she had promised. After her death the woman came to haunt her daughter. But when the daughter went on pilgrimage for her mother, she had to carry the ghost the whole way. To prevent that, she should have said, "You go ahead, mother."
175593: A werewolf was a man who had draped a cowhide over himself. A man coming home late in the evening was jumped by a werewolf. The werewolf made itself carried until the man was almost home.
175596: On the Bessemer near V., a man on his deathbed had said: "Keep what you have, I will suffer what I can." One day a cow stood in front of the window. When a large black dog had come to lie under the table, a friar was called in. After the friar had read his prayers, someone had to lead the dog on a cord. Suddenly, however, the dog vanished without a trace. The boy still had the cord in his hand.
175599: The vuurman (fire-man) had set the mane of Jang's horse on fire.
175610: A witch from the Kastanjelarenstraat was visiting a family and said to the woman: "Your husband is the only one in this house who hasn't had any trouble yet". The next day the man was badly burned in an explosion at his work in Liège. When the witch came to visit again some time later, she said to the woman: "Well, well, is that Mr S.?"
175627: A boy went to steal grapes from the chaplain while his mother kept watch. When the mother saw a black cat brushing against her legs, she did not dare to move because she feared the cat was a witch. A little later her son came back without grapes. He had fallen into the cesspit.
175635: A man coming back from the mill in Offelken was followed by something strange.
175646: A farmhand of Muurkeshof was sent away so that the farmer could meanwhile burn his collar. When the farmhand came back, he was delivered from being a werewolf.
175658: A witch who lived on the Heide saw three boys riding on one bicycle to the fair in Meerheike. Then the witch said: "Well, well, three on one bicycle. That can't be allowed any more!" The witch struck once with her stick. The next moment the boys fell off their bicycle.
175661: A child had been given a sweet by an old woman. The mother forbade the child to eat the sweet, because she suspected the woman was a witch.
175673: Some people walking to Tongeren saw a coach standing by the inn 'Het Witte Paard'. The coach always stood still in front of that inn, while passers-by had the impression it was driving fast. They were ghosts who had no rest.
175680: A boy had read in a little book how to make mice. When the boy showed off his skills at school, he was taken to a friar. After the friar had read prayers over the boy, the child could no longer make mice.
175704: At a farmer's in Tessenderlo all the cows died. At midnight a voice was always heard shouting: "Sit still, wench!" The witch master of Diest said to the farmer: "One has already been to see you. Luckily you didn't give her anything from the big heap (?), or she would have gained even more power". Because the witch master was powerless, the people went to Hasselt, where they had to pray for nine days to Saint Anthony and Saint Benedict. From the ninth day on, no more cows died at the farmer's. The man now fed his animals grain, which made them very fat.
175706: A man coming back from Gestel saw fire flying out of a brook. In Tiewinkel the man saw a horse coming towards him.
175714: In Gors-Opleeuw the dead baron came back to haunt his estate. People were so frightened that they had a friar come to banish the ghost. A stable hand had to drag a chain across the estate without looking back. When the stable hand did look back once, he saw a little light hanging on the chain. That light was the baron's spirit, which kept crying "Ai, ai". After the ghost was banished, it was never seen again.
175715: A man was working on the Heikant when suddenly a little sheep came running up. The man tried to catch the sheep, but the animal always managed to escape. The sheep kept running in circles around the man.
175730: In the old days a black lady whose dress made a rustling sound used to come to Herderen.
175731: Mina had been visiting somewhere and had held a child on her lap all afternoon. That night the child did nothing but scream. Whenever her mother was not with her, the daughter claimed that someone was throwing the curtains about. Because the problem continued on the following nights too, the child had prayers said over her.
175733: A mother and father had put their little son's cot in their bedroom. Suddenly they heard three knocks under the child's bed. Strangely enough, there was nothing to be seen.
175735: Hoekelemie, a little woman who lived on the Berg, was often ridden at night by the maar (nightmare spirit). When Hoekelemie held a pocketknife above her chest in bed, she was no longer troubled by the maar.
175737: A witch from Sint-Truiden could infest people with white lice.
175739: A young man was walking along the paved road from Overrepen to Neerrepen. At the brickworks he was suddenly held back by a strange force, so that he had to turn back. When another man went with the boy, he could get through.
175744: A family had three children who had all died. One day the father went to Maastricht with a wheelbarrow. When on the way he met the witch who was responsible for the misfortune, he gave her a sound thrashing with a leather belt. After that the family had no more misfortune.
175747: In a fen in Helchteren lay a sunken bell that rang twelve at midnight. The bell had been thrown into the fen during the French period.
175752: On a farm in Waterloos worked a stable hand and a cowherd boy. Because the cowherd was always tired and kept getting thinner, the stable hand asked him one day: "What on earth is the matter with you?", to which the cowherd replied: "If you had to do at night what I have to do, you would get thin too!" The cowherd told his companion that every night he was saddled by a hideous woman, who rode him to Aachen. After the cowherd's feet had been shod in Aachen, he had to carry the woman back again. The stable hand suggested they swap beds the next night so that he would lie in the cowherd's place. When the woman came flying in at midnight, the stable hand struck her with a dung fork. The next morning the cowherd and the stable hand went downstairs for breakfast. Because the farmer's wife was nowhere to be seen and the farmer had made the food himself, the two boys asked: "Is the missus ill?", to which the farmer replied: "No, she probably got up during the night and broke her arm." The stable hand and the cowherd quit that very same day.
175756: Farmer H., who lived on the Kiewit in Gellik, went to the meadow with a cart and three horses. Although the cart was empty, the horses could go no further because they had to pass a witch's house.
175760: Anyone plagued by rats through the doing of a witch or a sorcerer had to walk around the house three times praying and leave an opening in the house through which the rats could escape.
175779: One night something strange happened in the house of Jaak P. When Jaak got up in the morning, all the crockery was broken, although he had heard nothing. Since then Jaak's house was called 'the haunted farm'.
175781: People who went to their girlfriends through the woods or across the heath in the evening were often jumped by the werewolf on the way. To deliver a werewolf, you had to take him to a hot oven twice.
175782: A monastery sank into the Grondelingenborn in Batsheers. One day a woman near the Grondelingenborn saw a thread coming out of the water and lying on the bank. The woman began to pull the thread and brought up a cross. Frightened, she cried: "Jesus, Mary!", and dropped the cross back into the water. Every year on Christmas night the bells were heard ringing from 'the other world'.
175784: A young girl who always went to a little chapel learned witchcraft from an old woman who owned a book of magic.
175794: One night the sorcerer Herme had to come to a crossroads near the Veldschip. A burning coach with four black horses would then appear. Herme had to ride along in the coach as far as the Brede Kapel. If he dared to look back, the devil would break his neck. When Herme arrived at the Brede Kapel, he was freed of his magic powers.
175799: Three poachers saw a hare running in the wood. When one of the poachers shot at the animal, the gun did not work. Then the hare cried: "The others have already gone through!" The animal was a witch.
175802: One day Bona van P. from Opheers went to Hoepertingen with some other people. They all wore a fine, freshly ironed smock. But a witch had made sure they were all full of lice, which crawled all over their bodies.
175819: Anyone who saw a black cat had to try to hit the animal with a club that had been dipped in holy water. A few days later one would then hear that some neighbour woman or other had become paralysed.
175827: The Trappists, the monks who now live in Achel, used to live on a farm in Neeroeteren. During the French Revolution the monks had a deed of sale drawn up, making the farm formally the property of a certain P. This administrative measure would prevent the French from seizing the monks' farm. When the danger had passed, however, P. refused to destroy the deed. Because P. would not give the farm back to the monks, he had to come back and haunt after his death.
175850: A witch was quarrelling with her sister-in-law. Out of revenge the witch made all the animals in her sister-in-law's stable die. Within a year and a half she also made five sons and one daughter of her sister-in-law die.
175852: A boy was walking with his girlfriend. Suddenly the boy said: "You go on ahead. If a werewolf comes up to you in a moment, you needn't be afraid, because it won't harm you." The boy put on his collar and roamed about as a werewolf for a while. Then he took his collar off again and walked on with his girlfriend.
175857: Some men coming back from the fair met a werewolf in Rutten. One of the men threw a red handkerchief at the beast's mouth. A little later they discovered that the werewolf was a friend of theirs, for he still had the red threads of the handkerchief between his teeth. Later the werewolf's skin was burnt, and so he was delivered.
175873: The doctor had fallen in front of the house of Anna, who was standing outside. "Did you fall, doctor?" said Anna. The man replied: "If you hadn't been standing outside, I wouldn't have fallen".
175891: A certain M. from Beringen had black pigs. The animals got the roofziekte (a wasting disease of pigs) because M.'s mother was a witch.
175899: A man from Overrepen was walking back from the fair in Rommershoven. On the way the man saw a big vuurman (fire-man) setting fire to the straw in the field.
175913: It was haunted by a barrier gate in a meadow. When a woman walked through the meadow at night and the gate opened by itself, she said: "God will reward you." Then a voice rang out: "Child, I have been waiting a hundred years for that reward from God." Since that night the meadow was no longer haunted. The dead one was released.
175917: An old woman was mowing grass in Hout when suddenly a gentleman came riding up on a horse. "I have lost a bag of money. Have you seen it, perhaps?" asked the gentleman. The woman, who had put the bag of money at the bottom of her basket, answered: "No, I don't have it." When the woman had died, she vanished inexplicably from her deathbed. From then on the woman haunted everywhere, crying: "Give it back, give it back, for down to the seventh generation the descendants will perish!" In the end a priest had to be called to banish the ghost. The person leading the ghost had to have nothing on his conscience.
175926: A man who was giving a feast went for a walk in the churchyard. The man knocked against some bones lying there and mockingly invited the dead person to his feast. When the guests were seated at table, there was suddenly a knock at the door. The servant went to open it and saw a monster standing there. The host told the servant to say that the company was already complete. But the dead man would not leave and said: "When someone is dead, his body decays, but you think the same happens to his soul. Believe me when I say that there is a judgement seat and an eternal fire and a pool of hell. That is where we lie burning." Then the dead man seized the host by the legs and smashed his head against the ground.
175930: A young man worked as a farmhand on a farm by the Maas. On Shrove Tuesday the young man rode somewhere with the horse. The next morning the horse lay dead in the stable. Strangely enough, the same thing happened again three years later. When the young man had been called because his father had died, he could not get his trousers fastened. By the door stood a woman who was said to be a witch. The fathers of Urmond came and said: "Never again put a living creature in this stable, for it is dangerous". The new horse was put somewhere else and stayed alive. But when a cow had calved, they were forced to house the animal in the dangerous stable. A few days later the stable began to rot.
175935: A man coming back from the tailor saw a black cat sitting on the gravel road near the Groemelingenstraat. A little further on, the man suddenly noticed that he no longer had the suit he had gone to collect from the tailor. The man went back and got his clothes back from someone who had picked them up from the road. When the man passed the Groemelingenstraat again, the cat was still sitting there. The man wanted to hit the animal, but remembered just in time that cats were often witches in disguise.
175939: A boy was courting a girl from Stein who was said to be a witch. One evening the boy went to his girlfriend late at night and pretended to be dead drunk. When the girl wanted to send him away at half past eleven, he pretended to have fallen asleep with his head on the table. That is how the boy saw the mother and daughter turn into cats at midnight and fly away through the chimney.
175941: A man was staying with a family in Gelinden but went elsewhere to spend the night. Yet Lucie saw the man walk through her room every night. She could not see the man's face. When the visitor had gone, Lucie no longer saw the ghost.
175945: A farmhand of the Negenoord was sent to Maastricht so that the farmer could meanwhile burn his collar, which hung on an apple tree. As soon as everything had burnt up, the farmhand was delivered.
175966: Because farmer H.'s sheep were all dying, the farmer went to the parish priest. The priest came to look and said: "If a woman comes asking for alms later, you must give her something." Later that day the farmer was visited by a beggar woman. Farmer H. said to the woman: "Wait a moment, I'll go and fetch you something." But the woman did not wait and took some straw that lay in front of the door. After that all of farmer H.'s sheep stayed healthy. That woman must have been a witch.
175968: Because there were always many cats in the Reikemerstraat, people went to the parish priest for advice. The priest said: "Those cats are the souls of unbaptized children. If you see cats again, you must sprinkle the animals with holy water and say: 'I baptize you in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost'. Then the cats will disappear."
175971: In the house of Lies B. there once lived a stingy farmer. The labourers who came to mow the field during the harvest were paid by the barrel. When the labourers went to eat at noon, the farmer secretly took away part of the grain, so that he had to pay less in the evening. When the farmer was dead, he had to come back to haunt. At first the ghost had the form of a duck that sat on the edge of the cesspit. Some time later the farmer had to haunt as a dog. That dog was so strong that it pushed the animals over in the stable. When the superior of the Monnebruurs (Friars Minor) wanted to exorcise the dog, the ghost reproached him for once having stolen pins. "Yes," the superior admitted, "but afterwards I put back twice as many pins." The friar exorcised the ghost until he was drenched in sweat. The ghost begged for rest, but the friar said: "For you there is no rest anywhere, except in the eternal damnation of hell!" Then the ghost was banished to a timber yard.
175985: On the Sint-Truidensteenweg in Hasselt stands a castle in which a window is missing. Because the devil is said to have flown out through that window, it has never been possible to fit a new pane in it.
175994: In the garden of the C. family, where the town hall was later built, there used to be thorn bushes and little birch trees. On summer evenings around eleven o'clock the wind always began to blow so hard in that garden that people thought the little trees would be blown over. No one ever knew where that mysterious wind came from.
176004: Because Mones C. had unlawfully taken a lot of money, he had to haunt after his death. The drossaard (bailiff) would appear with a glowing pen behind his ears and come into the house in the shape of a big black dog. The dog knocked all sorts of things over. Seven or nine clergymen (1) read texts aloud from a big book. Then they led the ghost along the chapel road to 't Hoxent in Kerkhoven, where he was banished for ninety-nine years.
176012: A man leaving for work saw an altar standing next to his house. When the man came home the next day, the altar had disappeared.
176021: The little castle of H. at the crossroads on the road to Stevoort was haunted. For instance, there was a window that could not be closed in any way; the next day the glass was always out of it again. A brave man who dared to go into the little castle decided to bake cakes there. Suddenly, however, a voice rang out from the chimney, saying: "Are the cakes nearly done?" At that the man ran home scared to death.
176022: In the north of 's Heerenelderen there is a pit, close to 'de Toevlucht' along the road to Mopertingen. On Christmas night people heard the bells of the sunken church of Tongeren ringing in that pit.
176023: One day a farmer was visited by a man who made him a business proposal. The farmer, at first very interested, noticed however that the man had strange feet. It was the devil. When the farmer made the sign of the cross, the man vanished at once.
176028: On a farm where all the animals were dying, the priest was sent for. The priest stood all alone in the stable to pray and fight the devil. After a while the devil flew out through the wall. There was a large hole in the wall and a terrible stench hung in the stable.
176044: A man knocked at an old woman's door and asked: "Don't you have any animals in your stable you want to sell?" The woman then took the man to the stable, patted him on the shoulder and said: "I have plenty of those goats!" When the man had left, he suddenly itched all over. He took off his coat and saw that the witch had given him lice.
176046: A man who was churning butter was visited by a woman who wanted to borrow all sorts of things. When the man refused, the woman said: "Just you keep on churning!" Because the man could no longer make butter, he went to the parish priest, who gave him a holy object to put under the threshold.
176057: A shepherd from Leut owned a band with which he could turn himself into a werewolf. When the band was thrown into the fire, the man was immediately standing by the oven to save the thing.
176066: At night the maar (nightmare spirit) came and lay on people, so that they could no longer breathe.
176072: The fireball floated about above the meadows in the village. One day the fireball had set a man's coat on fire.
176073: In the attic of the witch M., witches' gatherings were always held at night. Because M.'s husband could not sleep because of it, he once went upstairs to give the witches a good thrashing. The next day M. had only one arm left.
176087: In the house next to Heksebetje's lived weavers. Whenever the weavers were at work, the yarn became completely tangled because of the witch.
176088: In Heers there lived men who dealt with evil. They wore a cowhide on their backs and had the power to turn themselves into a werewolf. If you could make a werewolf bleed, he was freed.
176095: A mother saw a black cat lying in her child's cot. The mother had come in just in time, because the cat was about to smother the child.
176104: A man who was visiting a woman on a moonlit winter evening was nearly frightened to death when he heard a loud bang in the attic of the house. A little later the other woman who lived in the house came in. That must have been a witch.
176106:
In the Rekkerbroek there was a spring called the Grondeleer. At that spring a bell rang at exactly twelve o'clock on Christmas night. That night two men from Membruggen had gone to listen to the bells. Those two men never came back.
Where the church of Membruggen now stands, there used to be a temple where the idol Mem was worshipped. Because the village also had many bridges, it was given the name Membruggen.
When Sint-Servaas came to preach in Tongeren and the inhabitants refused to be converted, he said: "Heathen Tongeren will perish and Maastricht will rise."
When Tongeren perished, a chapel with a bell sank into the Grondeleer. That is why a bell is still heard ringing there every year on Christmas night.
176109: On the Keiberg a man met a witch, who said: "You need not be afraid of me. You must not believe everything they say about me." The witch could read minds.
176110: In Neerweert there was a haunted farmhouse. At midnight pots and pans could always be heard rattling there. Because the neighbours could not sleep at night, the house was eventually torn down.
176123: When Roos was going home, she saw near a cave a haystack standing in the middle of the road and moving along. The next day the haystack was gone and at that mysterious spot Roos saw a well and a thorn bush.
176137: On a farm in Eigenbilzen the cows were always untied at night. When a friar was called in, the clergyman said: "Take a spade and dig a hole in front of the manger." In the ground they found a fat toad. After the friar had said prayers over the creature, the farmer had no more trouble.
176153: A boy from Aldeneik had gone to visit his fiancée. When the boy came home in the evening, he had to walk through water the whole time. The girl had done that to him.
176157: Bailiff Clerckx came from Eksel or Neerpelt. He lived in a house on 't Hobos (Hoogbos), a hamlet of Overpelt. Along the Meuse, bailiff Clerckx wiped out the bokkenrijders (goat riders, a gang of robbers said to ride goats through the air) on the orders of the prince-bishop. Near 't Hobos the bailiff was later seen flying through the air in a fiery coach.
176163: When Mieke V.D.F. came back from Hees, she was always followed by C. the werewolf. Sometimes the werewolf appeared in the shape of a big black dog, at other times in the shape of a foal. Sometimes Mieke had to carry the werewolf until she reached the first houses of Vlijtingen. That werewolf had sold his soul to the devil.
176165: Some soldiers standing guard at the border between Belgium and the Netherlands saw a woman with long hair and a long dress appear between midnight and one o'clock. The woman walked across the border while combing her hair. Then one of the soldiers said: "If you are good, speak. If you are evil, vanish!" The next moment the woman had vanished.
176166: Old Brouns was convinced that Mie had turned a child's little head back to front. He went after the witch and forced her to set the head straight again.
176187: At the castle of Wijer, the shades of the former inhabitants were seen searching for treasure at night.
176198: A farmer whose wife was bewitched sent for the "menneke van Genk" (the little man of Genk). The little man transferred the evil hand to a dog. When the farmer stood ready at twelve o'clock the next day to catch the spirit, the dog was standing there.
176202: A man went to his uncle Leo, who lived only a kilometre and a half away. After wandering about for two hours, the man ended up back at his own house. When his brother went with him, the man reached his uncle in five minutes.
176207: Every Saturday a boy was afflicted by a strange ailment. The boy would come downstairs and then sit motionless for a long time. After the boy's brother and father had been to the 'three Sisters' of Sint-Truiden, the boy behaved normally again.
176216: At Danekwijt in the meadows people did not dare to go and fetch animals, because they were held back there by a ghost.
176217: In Kerniel there lived a boy who could make mice in the church. After the priest had baptised the boy, the devil no longer had any power over the child.
176219: The wife of Mil B. was a witch. All night long Mil was covered in feathers. In the morning all the feathers had disappeared.
176223: A man coming back from Viersel saw a large ghostly figure standing on the road.
176238: In Schalkhoven a black cat used to roam about. People were afraid of the cat because they believed the animal was the apparition of an old man who had died long ago.
176240: Alma, Kait's daughter, had an inflamed finger. When the girl came back from the doctor, she met a woman who advised her to go and see her mother Kait. People suspected that Alma was being bewitched by her own mother. So Alma went to her mother, who said: "You thought you didn't need your mother any more, didn't you, but now you see!"
176242: A farmer had a farmhand who was a werewolf. When the farmer had thrown the farmhand's collar into the oven, the boy was instantly standing beside him because he wanted to pull the collar out of the fire. The farmer had the greatest trouble holding the boy back. When the collar had burnt up, the farmhand said: "I am willing to work for you a year for free, that is how happy I am now."
176243: One night a certain Gerard F. had to take meat from Peer to Weert. Gerard was terrified when, in the woods of Dorplein, a fierce fire suddenly broke out. In the distance Gerard saw the fire-man stride across the heath, shaking sparks off himself the whole time. Then the fire-man went on his way.
176245: Old P. was nearly scared to death when he saw the friend he was talking with suddenly change into a dog. Because P. was attacked by the dog, he quickly threw a red handkerchief at the animal's mouth.
176254: A man was annoyed that there were always cats howling in his attic. One day the man hit the cats with a stick. In doing so he broke his own wife's arm.
176260: Some men who saw a mysterious figure on the road to Herk asked: "What time is it?" But there was no answer.
176261: A man who had been to the shop in Roy lost his way on the way back because of a black dog sitting at the side of the road. Only when the man reached the oak wood could he find his bearings again.
176264: A man from Ophoven struck at a cat with a dung fork. The next moment his wife lay on the ground with a broken arm. That is how the man found out that his wife was a witch.
176265: Anyone who was touched by a witch was afterwards completely covered in lice.
176268: When Richard N. was driving across the heath in the evening to take a load to a camp, he was jumped by a werewolf. Richard got lost and did not find his way back until morning.
176271: A schoolmaster going home in the evening was jumped by a werewolf on the way. The werewolf turned out to be someone the schoolmaster knew well.
176283: A boy who had gone to visit his girlfriend in Zonhoven was followed by a cat on the way back. When the boy hit the cat on the head, the animal got a swelling. The boy then asked: "What's the matter with you?" No sooner had he spoken than the cat scratched his face.
176285: Someone who had been unable to keep a vow before his death came back to haunt so that the vow could still be carried out, by himself or by others.
176286: Gjotter knocked at a woman's door and asked whether she was troubled by mice, to which the woman replied: "Yes, sometimes." Gjotter then gave her this advice: "Here is some blessed earth. Scatter the earth where the mice are, and then they will run away." The woman took the earth and followed Gjotter's advice. A few days later the woman was plagued by hundreds of mice.
176289: In Mopertingen lived a man called 'den Houten'. That man drank a lot and kept saying: "Little foot, you may go barefoot. Little throat, you may stay dry." When the man went home one night, he sat down on a calf that grew bigger and bigger. At the Bergkuik in Waltwilder the calf threw the man to the ground. That calf was a werewolf.
176291: A man walking along the Houterestraat to the wood of Suska one evening saw will-o'-the-wisps floating ahead of him. When the man had almost reached Maria V.M., the will-o'-the-wisps changed direction and flew to the wood of Z. People believed that will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children, floating between heaven and earth.
176295: A man coming back from the pub saw a big sheep near the Oppenhof. The man could not catch the sheep. The animal followed the man all the way to his house. Then the sheep suddenly vanished.
176305: A man who had vowed to go on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel or to Kortenbos had died. After his death the man had to haunt because he had not kept his vow. The ghost was invisible to everyone except the dead man's niece. The girl went on pilgrimage together with the ghost of her dead uncle. After that the ghost did not show itself any more.
176310: Someone had bought a heifer in Schakkebroek. After a witch had stroked the heifer with her hand, the animal was full of lice. In the end the cow died.
176314: A girl limped after a witch had stepped on her foot. The friars could not cure the girl because the witch herself was not present.
176328: A man going to the brewery in Vreren saw a big black dog in the Kellesteeg, which wagged its tail in the man's face. A boy who had heard the man's story wanted to see the dog for himself. When the boy reached the dog, he said to the animal: "Don't come over here, little fellow!" Because the dog followed the boy anyway, the boy threw a red handkerchief at the animal. At that the dog ran off. For the devil is afraid of a red handkerchief.
176335: After Vloekskus had been bewitched by a woman from Hasselt, he had trouble with his eyes. Someone advised him to roast a black hen on the fire for nine days. During that time no one was allowed to come and ask him for something he did not have. On the sixth day a woman came asking for a bunch of grapes. Because Vloekskus did not have any, his eyes were not healed.
176350: A man was coming back from the market in Tongeren with a pig. On the way he met a woman, who walked part of the way with him. Before the man got home, the pig was dead.
176352: A farmer's cart had got stuck just as a witch was passing by. When the farmer struck the spokes of the wheel with a stick, the witch cried: "Stop hitting; I'll let you go on!" After that the cart moved off without any trouble.
176376: Three poachers met a ghostly badger at night.
176388: A woman often came to a family in Widooie to ask for a slice of bread. One day the woman asked the little boy who opened the door: "How is your little brother?", to which the boy answered: "I don't have one yet". When the boy's brother was born some time later, he cried all the time. The child only stopped crying when he was taken out of the cradle. In the end the parents decided to go to the friars with the baby. The friars cut open the pillow and found that it was full of pins.
176392: When the washing had been done, the witches came and tied knots in the laundry.
176394: One day a family from Boorsem was visited by a woman who came peddling. After they had sent her away without buying anything, the family had misfortune with the animals and the harvest. A friar had come to say prayers over the farm, but that had not helped. Because the people were convinced that Lies, the witch from Rekem, was responsible for the misfortune, they moved to the Ardennes.
176415: A man who worked at the castle of Genoelselderen saw a big black cat sitting on the wall every evening. Whenever the man walked along the wall, the cat went along with him. When one day the man knocked the cat off the wall, the animal came after him.
176418: On a farm in Beverst they always had misfortune with the cows. One night a witch was seen standing behind one of the cows.
176458: A vuurman (fire man) was a lost soul. A man coming home at night from the fair in Heur saw a fire moving up and down by a linden tree. Then the fire moved across Moas's field towards a wood.
176459: The mayor of Wellen had a child who was bewitched: the child's toes were where its heels should be. The parents did not know what to do and were advised to go to a fortune teller. So they went to Rikus J. in Maastricht. Rikus went home with the parents to free the child from the witchcraft. On the way, in a wood, Rikus said: "In this wood lives someone who was banished for 99 years. He is tied up with a red silk thread. Shall I let him loose?", to which the parents said: "No, no, please don't!" Once home, Rikus began reading aloud from a little book, warning the parents: "Soon the witch will come and knock on the door, but you must not let her in, and you must not ask who is there either, because then the witch will make herself invisible." A little later they heard someone knock on the door, and the woman asked: "Who's there?" She opened the door but saw no one. By reading from the little book, Rikus finally managed to set the child's feet straight. Afterwards they could guess who the witch was. A good while later a woman died in the village whose body could not be taken to the church: the horses would not pull it. Then they harnessed the horses behind the cart, and then they did walk to the church. Among them was one horse that was pitch black and kept foaming at the mouth.
176462: A man coming home at night saw a strange figure that was white at the top and black at the bottom. Suddenly the figure was gone. A little later the man saw the strange apparition again. The man went mad.
176463: The man who drove the mail coach from Maastricht to Hasselt got lost in the Platvijver. The man spent the night with a certain Janneke, who murdered and robbed him. The murdered man came to haunt near the Platvijver. Janneke lived for a long time on the stolen money. When he lay on his deathbed, his children suggested giving the money back after all. To this Janneke said: "Keep what you have, and I will suffer what I can." Shortly after Janneke's death a ghost wandered about the Platvijver, crying: "Give it back, give it back!" The friars dragged the ghost with chains to a bush in the Maten and banished it for ninety-nine years and more.
176480: A man who went to herd the cows in the marsh always heard a strange rustling and saw a dead person return in the wood. After people had prayed, the dead person no longer appeared.
176499: At 'Canada', a farm near the chapel of Oetshoven, there was haunting because the former owner had committed suicide.
176505: At night a lady in a white silk dress drove along the castle lane in a black coach with two white horses. When the lady reached the castle farm, the gates opened by themselves.
176512: A family went to pray in Maastricht to be freed from witchcraft. When they were going back home, they met their neighbour, who said: "Are you back from Maastricht already?" The people had never trusted their neighbour.
176517: In Niel a bird was found. The bewitched child died.
176524: When the old parish priest of the Grote-Hei went to Achel, he got lost, although he knew the way very well. The next day the priest gave Trien G. a beating without a word of explanation.
176529: A boy coming back from Eksel on a winter evening saw a cat sitting on a narrow little bridge. Because the boy was afraid of the animal, he said: "Get off that bridge, because I have to go home!" The cat, however, stayed sitting there unperturbed. Then the man took out his stick and knocked the cat into the brook. A second later the animal was already back on the bridge. The man struck a second time. When the man wanted to knock the cat off the bridge for the third time, the animal said: "Strike me again now if you dare!" The man was so frightened that he went home by another way.
176547: A shepherd who had been to Maastricht with his sheep had pushed a witch's cat off a turnstile. The cat followed the man all the way to the farm where he lived.
176549: Every day at about the same time a hare came running into the house of Neel J. in Dorplein. One day Neel asked Karel P., a poacher, whether he would come and shoot the hare. But when Karel had fired a shot, the hare sat there motionless. The next day the animal did not turn up any more.
176551: Witches' gatherings were often held in Vrijheers, in Renotte's meadow opposite the farm of the old mayor. A farmer who lived close to the meadow had one day taken part in the witches' feast of food and drink. Because he had enjoyed the gathering so much, he decided to go there every day. One day, however, the farmer had to sneeze and then said carelessly: "God bless me." The next moment all the witches had vanished and the farmer stood alone in the meadow. Since then he never again had the chance to take part in a witches' gathering. The farmer found this a great pity, for there was nothing he liked better than drinking along with someone for free.
176559: Old D. came back to haunt in Suslommel (?).
176577: A boy had heard it said that his girlfriend was a witch. The boy had already kept watch at the girl's window several times to see what happened there. One evening the boy saw his girlfriend and her mother rubbing themselves with ointment from a little pot. Then they sat on a broom and spoke the following magic formula: "Over hedges and hawthorns to the wine cellar of the priest of Cologne", and they flew through the air. The boy had watched closely where the women had hidden the pot of ointment, and when they were gone, he wanted to try the whole ritual himself. The boy rubbed himself with witch's grease and said: "Through hedges and hawthorns to my sweetheart in the wine cellar". When the boy arrived in the wine cellar, he was badly hurt. But his girlfriend and her mother took good care of him. After their wine feast, he asked: "How are we going to get home now?", to which the girl's mother replied: "Something will come along." A little later a black dog came running up. The boy's girlfriend and her mother sat on the animal's back. Because there was no room left for the boy, the mother said to the animal: "Tie, stick out your tail!" The boy sat on the animal's tail, after the mother warned him: "Take care not to speak the Sweet Name!" Then the dog rose high into the air. But when the three flew over the Rhine, the boy became frightened and cried: "Oh God, oh God!" At once the dog dropped its tail, so that the boy fell down. Luckily they had just crossed the water, so the boy could still walk back home.
176579: A man walked past a barrier on which a cat was sitting. When the man said: "Hello, pussycat", the cat replied: "Lambert said to me: 'Pussycat, where are you going?'"
176585: A man cycling back from Achel was jumped on by a black cat. Since the man could not chase the angry cat away, he jumped off his bicycle and fled to a nearby house. When the man dared to come out again after half an hour, the cat had vanished.
176589: Some men came into a house full of cats. A wizard said: "If I say one of the cats must go up the chimney, she will do it." And so it happened. When the men went home, they lost their way.
176595: On L.'s farm in 't Hasselt the animals made noise every evening. Some animals even died. After the parish priest had blessed the farm and said prayers over it, they were no longer troubled by the evil hand.
176603: Janneke van de Platvijver had to come back to haunt after his death because he had murdered and robbed someone. Because the ghost kept crying: "Give it back, give it back!", the friars banished Janneke to the Maten.
176607: On the Vranckenpoort along the road from Opoeteren to Neeroeteren a strange animal often sat that frightened people.
176609: People used to believe that a castle in Maasmechelen was haunted. When the castle was demolished, a money box was found walled up in a wall. The woman to whom the box was given immediately asked: "Have you got the ghost?"
176610: A man had promised his wife to go on pilgrimage in honour of Our Lady. Because the man had not kept his promise, his wife came back to haunt after her death. When the man had gone on pilgrimage, the ghost was released.
176637: In the time of Saint Willibrord there was a small church in Sint Ool (in Dorne). The bell hanging in the tower, however, had not been consecrated and fell into a peat pit. When people had almost hoisted the bell out of the pit, an old woman came by and said: "There's that damned witch now!" At that the bell fell back into the pit. Every year on Christmas night at exactly twelve o'clock the bell is heard ringing from under the ground. Because everyone was afraid to visit the place, a man made a bet with his friends. He had to go to the place where the bell had hung and bring back a twig of a hawthorn and of a lime tree as proof to show his friends. The man did it, but when he returned he advised everyone never to go to that place.
176651: Some people saw a mouse running around wearing a wedding ring around its belly. When the mouse had been struck, a neighbour woman was suddenly standing beside them.
176654: In the cellar of a farm near Viersel stood a chest in which a ghost had been banished. The dead farmer came haunting because his sisters had not given the farm to Pee V., the lawful heir. As a ghost the farmer came to throw his sisters out of their beds. The animals in the stable were always untied and eventually died. The parish priest banished the spirit into a chest that was walled up in the cellar. Later the chest was moved to the sacristy of Viersel, where it was kept for its value as an antique.
176663: In the Brouwersstraat lived a family with seven sons. One of the sons had developed a hunchback shortly after his birth. His brothers were convinced that a witch had caused this disability. When the witch once came to visit, the boys put a little straw cross by every door, so that the witch could not get out. The woman had announced several times that she was going home, but each time she reached the door she turned back. One of the sons began to lose patience and said to the witch: "If you can't go outside, then you must undo the evil you have done here!" At first the witch denied any guilt, but in the end she stroked the boy's hump. A short time later the hump had disappeared.
176670: When the bailiff Clercx was dead, he was banished under a bridge in Kerkhoven (a hamlet of Lommel). The bailiff's estate then passed into the possession of a notary from Tongeren.
176679: Some people from Gessel wore a black neckerchief on their heads to go to the mill. When they arrived they were sweating so much that they took the cloth off their heads. When the people got home, they saw that their neckerchiefs were full of lice.
176688: On the Muizehei there used to appear half a priest wearing a gown and a large black hat. Because people were afraid of the floating priest, they went to ask the dean for advice. "You must baptise him," said the dean. After that was done, the priest was never seen again.
176691: In a forest between Mol and Antwerpen lived a boy who had never done any work. When the boy did his military service, he got to know other boys who were all learning a trade that gave them great satisfaction. On returning home the boy announced that he wanted to go to America. Before taking the boat in Antwerpen, the boy went into a little chapel, where he lit a candle for Our Lady. Suddenly the boy saw the devil sitting under the feet of the statue of Mary and thought to himself: "The devil is all alone after all; I'll light a candle for him too." Then the boy left on the boat. After earning money in America for seven years, the boy decided to visit his parents. On arriving in Antwerpen, the boy looked for a place to spend the night, since it was already too late to get home. The people who gave the boy lodging suspected that their guest was carrying a lot of money in his heavy trunk. The landlady said to her husband: "That fellow has a lot of money. If we murdered him, all that money would be ours and we wouldn't have to sell all our belongings!" Because the man could not bring himself to murder someone for money, he decided to handle it differently. The man and the woman counted the money in the trunk and neatly wrote down all the details on a sheet. The next day they gave their guest his trunk back. Then the boy rode off on horseback to the station. The boy had barely left when the man and the woman notified the police and said: "The boy who stayed with us last night has robbed us. We have written down exactly what has gone missing." On arriving at the station the boy was arrested and thrown into prison. In his cell the innocent boy was visited by the devil, who said: "If you sell your soul to me, I'll get you out of here." Because the boy had never had the chance to go to church in America, he did not want to accept the devil's offer. Then the devil said: "What you did for me, no one has ever done. Because you lit a candle for me, I will help you. When the trial begins tomorrow, you must ask for a delay and say that you are still expecting a lawyer." When the boy had been granted an hour's delay, everyone sat looking tensely out of the window. A little later a figure dressed in red came riding up on a black horse. The lawyer said: "Money can be counted and paper can be written on!" Then he drew a circle on the ground and ordered the accused and the accuser to stand in the circle. "In a moment the devil will come and fetch the guilty one out of the circle," said the lawyer. A little later the devil broke the dishonest man's neck and took him away. Later the man's head was found on a dung heap in the field. When the innocent boy asked for his money, the judge answered: "Yes, but the costs of the trial still have to be paid." These words had barely been spoken when the boy said: "If you don't give it to me, I'll make him come again!" At that the boy got his money immediately.
176693: A werewolf was a man who owned a special band with which he could turn himself into a black dog. One day a man on his way to work met a black dog. The dog quickly snatched the man's red handkerchief. Further on, the man went into a café for a drink to recover from the fright. One of the customers still had the red threads of the handkerchief between his teeth.
176699: At midnight a woman saw a white spirit appear on the Akker. The spirit asked the woman to pray for him. When the woman had done so, the spirit was not seen again.
176703: Because the miller of Lauw had stolen a great deal during his life, after his death he had to haunt in the shape of a devilish black dog. The dog danced constantly on the water of the Jeker and then climbed up the mill wheel. A young priest from Rutten came to the mill to banish the ghost. But when the priest made the devil appear, it said: "You cannot banish me, for you once stole a cabbage yourself." The priest replied: "That is true, but I left a franc in its place." After that the priest succeeded in banishing the ghost.
176706: A man coming back from visiting his girlfriend met a strange black apparition at the old hollow walnut tree. When the man was a little further on, he turned around and said: "Speak!", but no answer came. A hundred metres further the man was startled by the sound of a magpie. By the church of Overrepen, in the Drekstraat, the man saw a whole pack of screeching cats. As the terrified man walked on, some of the cats leapt at him. The man hurried home and told his mother about the mortal fear he had suffered. The Drekstraat was haunted.
176708: Soldiers on guard had to call out three times before they were allowed to fire a shot. The soldiers had often seen a pig walking about at night and had not managed to shoot the animal. Then another soldier said: "Let me keep watch for once." As soon as the pig came along, the man called: "One-three", and shot the pig dead. The pig turned out to be the commander of the army.
176714: The shopkeeper's daughter had a large wound on her back that would not heal. At midnight a gentleman and a woman from Antwerp came to look at the girl. The gentleman and the woman found that the girl had 'a point of blood' (?) too little. The shopkeeper was given a prayer card with a prayer he had to say nine days in a row. "Doesn't a strange woman often come to the shop?" the people from Antwerp had asked. The shopkeeper had replied: "Yes, there is someone who always comes and stands here with her arms crossed and quite likes a chat." The people from Antwerp then said: "Keep her out, for she is the one!" The gentleman and the woman had barely left when the wound began to heal. From that night on the witch was no longer allowed in the shop.
176719: A woman and her son had visited M. In the evening M.'s child began to wail. The child had probably been bewitched.
176721: A man walking through Nietelbroeke in the evening suddenly saw a snow-white rabbit running. The man caught the rabbit and wrapped it in his blue smock. When the man opened the smock a little further on, he found a skull there. After the man had thrown the skull away, it turned back into a rabbit.
176722: In Stamprooi a newborn baby died after it had been stroked by a witch.
176728: A man who was manuring the field struck with his dung fork at a magpie sitting in the field. The magpie turned out to be a woman from the neighbourhood.
176733: At Fien P.'s house the paintings rattled against the wall in the evening. The witches were in the house then.
176742: A cat used to haunt the Steenberg near the chapel of Hilst. A man coming back with his friend Marneffe from a visit to Polleke Flips was followed by a cat that kept running between his legs. The men did not dare kick the cat.
176744: In the garden of the M. family a hare sat nibbling the cabbages. The father, who was a hunter, shot the animal. It was his own daughter, who had turned herself into a hare.
176746: A woman standing with her foal in a field saw a white lady appear.
176748: A farmer had a farmhand who had made a pact with the devil. The farmhand always went to the pub and drank five-cent shots all Sunday. As soon as the farmhand had spent his five cents, there were five more cents in his pocket. Usually the farmhand did not come home until twelve o'clock. When one day the lad came home at eleven, the farmer asked: "Well, why are you home so early?" The farmhand answered: "Go and look behind the grey mare. The devil is lying there." When the farmer indeed saw a big black dog lying behind the mare, he sent for the brown friars of Sint-Truiden. The friar, who arrived in the stable at a quarter to twelve, quickly began reading his prayers. The next moment the dog flew out through a hole in the wall. That hole could never be closed again. The farmhand left and never came back.
176753: Between Opitter and Tongerlo was a place called 'de Hel' (Hell), because a man possessed by the devil lived in a deep ditch there. In that ditch stood a hollow tree stump, in which the man hid a collar with which he could turn himself into a werewolf. In the evenings the werewolf leapt on passers-by and made them carry him. Some people who had spied on the werewolf went one day to fetch the collar and threw the thing into the oven. As soon as the band caught fire, the werewolf was already standing by the oven to save his possession. The werewolf managed to pull his collar out of the fire. When they tried the same thing a second time, the werewolf was not quick enough. As soon as his collar had burnt up, the werewolf cried joyfully: "Now I am delivered!"
176759: If people saw one magpie, they would have bad luck. If they saw three magpies, the family would receive big news.
176762: In Horpmaal a father had said to his daughter in a fit of rage: "I wish the devil would come and take you!" When the girl went to the shop with some friends that evening, she saw a black dog standing at the street corner. Her friends did not see the animal. Because their daughter had vanished without a trace by morning, the desperate parents went to a fortune teller, who said: "Look for your daughter; she is still on your farm." They did indeed find the girl on the straw in the barn. The child was immediately taken to the priest of Hendrieken, who had to put on a different habit three times to be able to help the girl.
176766: A woman whom a farmer's wife had called a witch said angrily: "You'll go to Hasselt with your butter, but you'll have to go through the water!" And so it happened.
176780: A woman could make mice without tails. One day the priest summoned the woman and asked her: "Now make some mice for me too." After a few moments dozens of little mice without tails appeared. The priest said: "Those mice are not perfect, because they have no tails," to which the woman replied: "Yes, I haven't got that far yet."
176783: In the cellar of the castle of Hengelhoef it was haunted during the winter. The cellar lay beneath the castle chapel. A gentleman and a lady from Brussels who stayed at the castle in summer found human bones in the cellar.
176784: A farmer who had three horses noticed that one of the animals stood exhausted in the stable every morning. One day the farmer saw a woman stroking the horse in the meadow. The farmer then decided to put his horses somewhere else during the day. From that day on the animals behaved normally.
176786: A man coming back from Stal one evening had no matches left to light his pipe. On the way the man saw fire on a black heap. When the man came closer, the heap walked away.
176800: In a shop in Schakkebroek worked a girl who was said to be a witch. When a woman asked the girl for a pound of rice, the girl replied: "Better ask for a pound of lice!" The next moment the woman was full of lice.
176803: A gardener worked at the castle of Wijer. One day a farmhand told the gardener that he often saw a ghost appear at night. A lady in a silk dress would come and stand beside the bed and stroke the farmhand's cheek. The gardener advised the farmhand to go and see a fortune teller in Sint-Truiden. The fortune teller explained to the farmhand that a treasure must be hidden somewhere, but that someone was standing in the way of its being found. The gardener and the farmhand searched for the treasure together for many days, but they never found anything.
176811: In the fen behind the church of Ophoven people often heard a bell ringing on Christmas night. French soldiers were said to have thrown the bell into the fen during the Revolution.
176818: When a man was going to his house in the Plantagestraat, he had to walk fast because the werewolf was after him and wanted to jump on him. On the rampart the werewolf stood laughing at the man.
176820: When a man was going to his house in the Plantagestraat, he had to walk fast because the werewolf was after him and wanted to jump on him. On the rampart the werewolf stood laughing at the man.
176834: A man went with five friends to the monastery of Jonckhold. The men were playing cards when at midnight the light suddenly went out. The men saw no one, but they were beaten black and blue by the Templars who came to haunt.
176843: Some people who had visited an aunt at the Buiting came back past the Gestel mill. When they met a big wolfhound, they hardly dared go any further.
176849: Some people had seen a fish flapping about on the road. The priest established that it was a ray and laid the creature on a handkerchief. The people were so frightened that they kept shouting: "Stab that fish with a dung fork!"
176853: A man driving a hay wagon past a witch's house suddenly could go no further.
176863: The werewolf was a kind of dog that jumped on people's backs. While the werewolf was being carried, it urinated on its victims until they were soaking wet.
176870: I once saw a werewolf from a distance. Werewolves can follow people, but they cannot cross crossroads and streams. Moreover, they never have more strength than the person they meet. A werewolf is a person who has made a pact with the devil for seven years. During that time he must regularly roam about as a werewolf for a number of hours. If you can make a werewolf bleed on his forehead - the place where he was baptised - he becomes human again and must start that seven-year period all over again. If you say: "The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us," you can also easily hold a werewolf by his collar, so that he chokes. That is how the Black Emperor of Rutten was choked. Whoever wants to become a werewolf himself will find a bearskin in the meadow that very evening, and is bound to the devil by a pact of seven years. Once you have become a werewolf, you are obliged in any case to serve the devil as a werewolf for seven years.
176876: Long ago in Budel there lived a farmer who often moved the boundary posts of his land to have a bigger field. When the farmer had died, he had to haunt with a post on his back. One evening a friar from Hamont advised the spirit to put the post back in its original place. Since then the ghost has not been seen again.
176882: The hunter W. had decided to catch a notorious werewolf from Briegden. Wijnand had asked twenty people from Gellik to surround the werewolf sitting on the dung heap. When W. wanted to shoot at the animal, his gun would not fire. The next day Wijnand shot a hare dead with that bullet. After the werewolf had been caught, his skin was thrown into the oven. As soon as everything had burnt up, L. said: "How happy I am that I am delivered!"
176889: A man who always played cards in the same pub one day saw a Dutchman make the playing cards fetch a bottle of gin.
176896: Some men had fetched hay on the Stijdbeemd by the Demer. But the men could not get home, because a witch or a werewolf had pulled the pin out of the cart's shaft. Around midnight the men nevertheless managed to remove the pin at a crossroads. Because the cart would no longer move, one of the men had to go home to look for another pin. But the man found nothing suitable, so he had to wait until the next morning to bring the hay home. The Fletersdal has always been haunted. If you did not make the sign of the cross with holy water there, you were sure to be bewitched.
176897: A farmer travelling with horse and cart suddenly could go no further. As soon as a woman had patted the horse on the back, the animal walked on effortlessly. From that day on people believed the woman was a witch.
176899: When Jef was coming back from Luik at about ten o'clock in the evening, he saw a man who was chopping wood and cutting fodder at the same time. Jan spoke to the strange man in French and in Dutch, but there was no response at all. In an inn a little further on, Jef told what had happened to him. The innkeeper answered: "Yes, things are not right there. Several people have already died at that spot".
176913: Young men who went to visit their girlfriends in the evening often saw will-o'-the-wisps on the way. Whoever followed a will-o'-the-wisp lost his way and ended up in a swamp.
176916: The witch with the white cap had given someone a white loaf. To be on the safe side, however, the bread was immediately thrown into the fire.
176957: In 'd' Enneke' lived people who were plagued by the evil hand. In the evening chains could be heard rattling near the horses and the cows. When the people came closer with a lantern, it went quiet again. In the end they had to sell the horse.
176967: A child from Dilsen had been given a little magic book by someone. After that the child could make mice from the earth of a molehill.
176972: A man sometimes saw a ghost in the Groemelingenstraat. Whenever the man stuck a knife blade-first into the ground, the ghost disappeared.
176978: In Lanaken lived a witch who often lured children with sweets and drinks. A wreath would then be found in the child's pillow. When the wreath was closed, the child died.
176995: A man coming back alone from Sint-Truiden at night saw a strange calf walking between Overbroek and Mechelen. The animal had a strange flicker in its eyes. When the man went to strike the calf, the animal suddenly vanished.
176996: A cowherd boy who worked on a farm had to fetch a dung hook from the smith one evening. When the boy was attacked by a werewolf on the way back, he struck the animal on the head with the dung hook. When the cowherd went to bed, he saw that the farmhand who slept next to him had a hole in his head. The next day the cowherd told the farmer that the farmhand was a werewolf. The farmer then sent the farmhand away and threw his animal skin into the oven.
176998: A man who had had his grain ground at the mill of Genk met a fire-man on the way back. The fire-man set the man's cart on fire.
177003: After the mayor had met a little old woman in the shop, his horses began to fight. A friar had to come and say prayers over the animals.
177010: Many horses and cows had died at a farmer's. When a woman set off for the mill at four in the morning, she saw a witch standing under an elm by the Lindeweg. "Woman, do you know what has happened?" asked the witch, to which the woman replied: "How should I know?" Then the witch said: "Here at the farmer's the horses have died.
177023: A man who was always followed by a cat on his way to work decided to take a club with him. The next time the man tried to hit the cat with the club. But he never managed to hit the cat.
177024: A man from Wezet saw a white figure appear in the wood. Because the man was a widower, he suspected the figure was his late wife.
177031: In Ordingen a werewolf always roamed about at night. The only way to stop a werewolf was to make him bleed.
177045: On a farm worked a farmhand who played the werewolf at night. Another farmhand who had grown suspicious told the farmer about the boy's strange behaviour. The farmer soon discovered the animal skin the farmhand had hidden behind the oven. After the animal skin had been burnt in the oven, the farmhand did not live much longer.
177050: At Kalverjan's on the Locht a werewolf with an animal skin always lay under the cart. During the midday meal the werewolf would stand with its paws against the windowsill. When one of the men had stabbed the animal with a knife, the werewolf changed into a human, who said: "I'm glad I've been freed. You must not betray me."
177055: A thick tree had been split open by lightning. A beautifully decorated little chapel hung on that tree. Strangely enough, the tree was undamaged at the level of the chapel. Below the chapel the crack continued.
177058: In a stable there was a black cat that meowed all the time and attacked everyone who came near her. Because the animals were afraid of the cat, the parish priest was sent for. The priest read prayers over the stable until the sweat dripped from his face. After the priest had prayed for a while, the cat walked outside and the animal was never seen again.
177076: In the pillow of a sick child a wreath of feathers was found that was not yet closed. If the wreath had been closed, the child would have died.
177083: A man walking home in the evening was frightened to death when he saw the devil's coach. The coach was surrounded by fire and was pulled by two large black horses.
177084: When Toon K. saw some cats sitting by the fire, he said: "Ah, little cats, go ahead and warm your little bottoms!" The animals replied: "If you hadn't spoken so nicely, we would have broken your neck!"
177092: In Sledderlo-Heide (Klein-Langerlo) there was a stone called 'the devil's claw', because it bore the imprint of a horse's hoof. Four times a year the stone became red-hot. The witch who lived behind one of the boulders would then sacrifice a human being on that stone. After many years a priest managed to drive the witch away by making the sign of the cross. The devil's claw rolled into a nearby pond.
177113: At S.'s there was a child that always started crying when it was put in its bed, and stopped crying as soon as it was picked up. The brown friars of Hasselt advised the parents to cut open the child's pillow. The wife of Geerke N. had stuck the pillow full of pins.
177120: A woman who lived by the witch house in Engsbergen heard a beautiful song in the evening. When people went outside to look, they saw nothing but cats. A man had wounded one of the cats with an axe. Two days later a woman in Schoten was ill.
177128: A man heard music in his attic and a noise as if a hundred horses were running about. Strangely, the children also got odd scratches on their skin. Because the parish priest could not help, they had the friars say prayers over the whole house. After that the witch had no more power.
177155: In Heers there was a black barrier with two mermaids depicted on it. People did not dare go near that barrier because they believed that a white lady in rustling clothes sometimes walked past. The lady did not speak a word.
177184: A man who had moved the boundary post of his field met, on his way back, the ghost of his father, who had been dead for ten years.
177188: A witch from Kuttekoven could turn herself into a cat.
177194: A boy from Corswarem heard all sorts of noises at night in the horse stable where he slept. In the morning the words "Pray, pray, pray" were written on the door.
177208: Frans had an animal skin with which he went about as a werewolf to frighten people. One night the werewolf was wounded after someone struck him with an axe. As soon as the werewolf began to bleed, he took on his human form again. Frans fell to his knees and begged for forgiveness.
177214: A man had arranged with a miller to go poaching in the Broek at night. The man had been waiting by a tree for a while, but the miller did not turn up. A little later the man saw four piglets run past, followed by a black dog. When a violent storm then rose, the man went home.
177217: On a hill in Opoeteren sat a werewolf who was suspected to be Michiel G. The werewolf often made people carry it, licking them and sometimes urinating on them. Giel M., who also often had to carry the werewolf, one day cut the animal with a knife, after which the werewolf no longer turned up.
177232: One day Trien C. was walking along the Kontveldstraat. When she came to the wooden gate of a meadow, she was amazed to see the gate open by itself. Trien said: "May God reward you in heaven for that", whereupon a voice replied: "For God's reward I have been sitting here for ten years." With her answer Trien had released the ghost.
177236: When the washing lay outside to bleach, people kept watch at night so that no one would come and steal it. Sometimes the 'knippers' (cutters) - invisible witches - came and cut the linen into a thousand pieces.
177238: A woman could conjure mice without tails from a heap of sand.
177245: Because a child was ill on Bolderberg, they went to the witch master of Hasselt, who said: "Doesn't an old woman come to your house every day and talk to the child?" When the man confirmed this, the witch master said: "Tomorrow the woman will come by again, but she will not come in." And so it happened.
177251: To drive away the maar (nightmare spirit), one had to lay one's socks crosswise on the bedside table. A man who often got cramps at night had been advised to put a piece of Sunlight soap and a piece of metal under the mattress, and only then lay his socks in the shape of a cross. This remedy, however, did not help the man.
177255: In Riksingen a certain Smets built a farm with a brewery next to it. During the following three years Smets had a great deal of misfortune: his wife died, the animals on his farm died one after another, and the farm burned down. Smets got help from his son-in-law, who had borrowed money and was very eager to rebuild the farm. But the tide would not turn: the farm burned down again. In the end Smets thought it wiser to rent the farm to a certain M. The brewery was converted into a manor house. M., however, turned out to have just as much misfortune: he died not long after moving into the farm. Smets sold the farm to Pee S., who was married to a woman from Sint-Truiden. Unfortunately Pee was not spared misfortune either: there was another fire on the farm. When Pee came home one evening, he saw a light in the manor house, but he did not dare go and look. Pee asked his wife: "Mieke, who is in the manor house? I saw a light burning there." Mieke answered: "There can't be anyone, because the key is hanging there on the wall." The next day Pee went to have a look in the manor house. Because the dust lay a finger thick, he concluded that indeed no one could have been there. Since Pee was still not entirely reassured, he visited the Brown Friars at the abbey in Tongeren. At first the friars did not take Pee's complaints seriously, but when the man kept insisting, the superior sent a friar home with him to say prayers over the farm and the manor house. The friar went praying through all the rooms of the house, but when he came to the gate, he suddenly lost his thread. The friar went round a second time, but this time in the other direction.
