When he came to the gate again, he could not get his words out: it seemed as if someone was holding him back. The friar went round for the third time, but again found the same thing. The friar said to Pee: "There must be something lying here that is holding me back. Call your workmen and have them break up the paving stones." While the workmen were doing this, they suddenly heard a strange sound. In the ground they found an enormous toad. When they had put the creature in a wheelbarrow, Timmermans came to photograph the toad. When the photo was developed, however, only an empty wheelbarrow could be seen: the toad was not visible. The toad was then taken to the Bornwei and thrown into the Born: the Born was so deep that no stick could reach the bottom. After that nothing strange happened at Pee S.'s again.
177260: Ann often looked after Frans M., the little son of Fin B. One day Ann was out walking with the pram when she suddenly met Zann. "What a beautiful child!" said Zann, and she stroked little Frans's legs. At that the baby began to cry loudly. Because the child would not stop crying, they finally had to go to the doctor. The baby had water on the knee and had to have an operation. Because of the problems with his knee, Frans was later exempted from military service.
177261: A man walking along the Ossenweg to Rummen heard an oak in Terkoest making strange noises. It seemed as if the oak was chewing the cud. It must have been the rustling of the leaves in the wind.
177262: Farmer Bert always had misfortune with his calves: they all died because they would not drink milk. The farmer decided to ask for help from the friars of Weert, with whom he always went along to Beek. Thanks to the friars' help, all the farmer's calves stayed alive.
177266: A man was out at night with his horse and cart. Suddenly a dog with a chain appeared, and the horse stood still. After the man had promised to give something to the poor, the dog was gone. A few days later the man's horse was attacked at night by the same dog. The man heard a voice say: "You did not keep your promise. Your horse will die here". Then the horse fell down dead, and the dog disappeared.
177272: A man who had danced with a witch all the way to Loon got lost and could not find the way to his house.
177292: When a farmer and his wife were coming back from Eisden, she heard kittens mewing in a bush. "Keep walking, those are witches," said the farmer. His wife replied: "No, those are kittens" and walked towards the bush. When she got closer, she found there was not a single kitten to be seen. When the woman and the man were ten metres further on, they saw a woman come out of the bush. The woman walked past the girls without saying good day. "See," said the farmer, "and you kept saying they were kittens!"
177296: On the Beukenberg there was a house that was haunted every evening.
177299: A little boy had developed a swelling on his leg after being bewitched by a big ugly woman. The boy and his family had to go on pilgrimage for nine Fridays to the Sint-Servaas church on the Vrijthof in Maastricht. After that the wound was healed.
177300: A farmer had a farmhand who was a werewolf. When the farmer had sent the farmhand to the field, he burnt the boy's collar. The moment the collar caught fire, the boy was immediately standing by the oven.
177325: A man had been to Hoelbeek with his dog to buy clogs. When the man went home in the evening, he was surrounded by cats. The dog behaved very strangely and did not dare catch a single cat. As soon as the man reached the boundary of Eigenbilzen, the dog behaved normally again.
177330: Two children could not sleep because they had been bewitched. After a friar had taken something out of their pillows, the children could sleep.
177347: Some men tending their animals in the meadows suddenly saw a white lady come out of the undergrowth. She was a witch.
177353: A man who went through the woods to his work in Waterschei was always followed by a strange light. The light frightened the man so much that he eventually went and bought a revolver.
177356: One evening three men went to fetch wood at the rag market. Because many witches roamed that market, people did not dare go there at night. When the men came back with their cart full of wood, one of them secretly made the horse stop so that the others would think a witch was involved.
177364: A man coming back from the fair with his friends saw a cat sitting on a post in Hechtel. Although his friends had advised him against it, the man struck at the animal with his stick. The man struck three times, but each time the cat jumped off the post. "Leave it alone now, you can see it's a witch," said the friends. The man did not dare strike a fourth time.
177371: In the Begijnhofstraat in Tongeren, some people believed they had seen a haunting beguine at night. When the roof of one of the little houses in the beguinage was renewed, a note from 1634 was found at the ridge, reading: "Go and search at the left corner of the stairs in the cellar; 600 Liège guilders are hidden there. Half is for the finder and the other half is to have masses said for my poor soul."
177376: In the Woestijnvijver in Diepenbeek bells were heard ringing at twelve o'clock on Christmas night.
177382: Some drunkards walking home at night suddenly saw two white nuns floating. One of the nuns said: "The night is not for people, but for ghosts." Shortly afterwards the nuns vanished again. The men were instantly sober.
177383: During a walk a girl asked her boyfriend whether he had a red handkerchief. If they met a werewolf, he was to throw the handkerchief at the beast's mouth. And so it happened. The next day the boy and girl saw a man who still had the threads of the red handkerchief between his teeth.
177386: A man sitting in the café said to his wife: "I'm going home. If you see a beast on the way, throw this handkerchief at its mouth." When the woman went home, she met a werewolf. She threw the handkerchief at the beast and then ran home quickly. The next day the woman saw that her husband still had the threads of the handkerchief between his teeth.
177401: At night a ghost in a white shirt appeared in the cemetery of Herk-de-Stad.
177409: S. had spent the whole evening helping Bollen in Beverst build a new house. When the man went back to Diepenbeek, he had to carry the werewolf.
177418: A man walking home alone one evening met a little dog in the Ougestraat that kept sitting down in front of his feet. After a while the man shouted in annoyance: "If you don't clear off, I'll kick you!" The man turned around and saw two cats sitting at the window of a house. Then the man decided to go home across the fields.
177426: In Wezent lived a woman who was suspected of being a witch. When a child was ill, a wreath was found in its pillow. Fortunately the wreath was not yet closed, otherwise the child would have died, according to the parish priest.
177427: When Janneke V. came home from his work at the factory in the evening, he saw a cat sitting on a turnstile. At home he said to his wife: "I saw a fine cat. There are quite a lot of mice here." On his wife's advice the man decided to bring the cat back with him the next day. He said to the cat: "Pussycat, where do you come from?" and picked the animal up. After a while, however, the cat started to grow heavier and heavier. When the animal fell out of Janneke's arms, it turned into a white lady, who said: "Janneke V., you asked me where I came from. Now here I stand. Now say what you want!" Janneke ran away as fast as he could.
177429: The 'kwade weide' (evil meadow) in Colmont was haunted. When a man drove past that meadow with his cart, the horse suddenly reared so wildly that the cart fell over.
177454: Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children. A farmer travelling with his cart said: "Hey, will-o'-the-wisp, if you come over here, I'll baptise you." The next moment the cart was completely full of will-o'-the-wisps.
177460: In the T. family in the Wilstraat in Rutten, the daughter had become pregnant through the doing of a witch.
177464: At the black Lieve Heer (crucifix) in Groenendaalbos something strange happened between midnight and one o'clock. A little black woman would be kneeling there, and she turned into fire.
177466:
A werewolf would jump on someone's back and make them carry it. If you could make a werewolf bleed, he was freed.
One day a man was jumped by a werewolf that was sitting on a fence. The man cut the werewolf on the head with a knife, after which the beast began to bleed. Later the man told who the werewolf was.
177475: In Paal there lived a little boy who could conjure mice by shaking a tree. After the priest had baptised the boy again, he could no longer make mice.
177479: On the Mulkenweg a black cat always sat in the evening, frightening people.
177491: A man from Rijkel had a fighting cock that performed excellently. One day a woman came to visit and took hold of the cock. After that the animal could no longer stand.
177500: A young mother was walking to Veerle with her child in her arms. On the way the mother met a woman, who said: "Come, let me have a look at your child". Shortly afterwards the child fell ill. After the child had been overlezen (prayed over to lift a spell), it recovered.
177502: When Giel climbed into a tree, he was suddenly soaking wet. "Come down quickly", said his father, "there is a witch in the tree who has made you wet!"
177506: Anyone who wanted to summon the ghost of a dead person had to tie a pound of polished copper to the ceiling with a string. The copper had to hang at face height when sitting on a chair. Then one had to put out the lights, close one's eyes and think of the person one wanted to see again.
177523: One evening a man was walking home past a bridge over the Nete between Lommel and Eksel. The man was chased for a good two hundred metres by the Drosser (drossaard, a bailiff), who tried to catch him. After his death the drossaard came back to haunt in the shape of a black dog with a chain around its neck.
177526: A man who had knocked a kitten off a turnstile was terrified to see some thousand cats appear.
177527: In an inn in Weert the devil had flown in through the window. When the devil had gone again, the priest was asked to read prayers over the inn. But no one managed to fit a new pane in the window anymore. Only when a friar had read prayers over the inn did it work.
177534: In the pillow of a sick child, people found a chain of feathers and wool.
177537: Tilman V. from Opheers went on a pilgrimage to Our Lady of 'Bon Secours' in Lantermangen. When the man left the chapel, a lady in a white silk dress came up and walked home arm in arm with him. The woman did not speak a word. When Tilman touched the gate of his house, the white lady suddenly vanished.
177539: In Tongeren the witches used oat grains that floated upright in the water to bewitch people. People who drank from the water were then bewitched.
177545: On the castle estate of Herkenrode the trees bent down to the ground when a haunting nun came flying by, coming to say something at the castle.
177547: A young man went to visit his girlfriend in Niel on the second day of Christmas. When the boy came back home, the leather of his shoes was completely ruined because he had to walk over the frozen towpath and could not get off it. His girlfriend was a witch.
177550: In Brustem there was a house that was bewitched. When the occupants sat praying the rosary by the stove in the evening, they always heard a fat rat with a long tail scratching at the door. When the rat made itself heard again one evening, the man opened the stove and threw the animal in. A little later someone came to tell him that Marjengenes, a woman from the village, was badly burned all over.
177563: A man had often seen a magpie sitting in a Canadian poplar. One day the man got out his gun and shot the bird dead. Later the man found that he had shot his wife Monique dead.
177568: During catechism class the priest had seen that Mie N. could make mice by throwing a little heap of sand on the ground. After prayers had been read over the girl at the presbytery, she could no longer make mice.
177571: Fien M. stood by a farmer's rabbit hutch and said she wanted to buy a rabbit. The farmer, however, did not want to sell his rabbits. That same evening a rabbit was missing from the hutch. A week later Fien told the farmer that she still had to pay for a rabbit. From then on the farmer no longer let Fien in.
177572: The priest did not know that his maid Trientje was a witch. Because Trientje was seriously ill and felt she was going to die, she asked the priest if she could confess. The maid admitted that she was a witch and that she was responsible for the deaths of many children and adults. "Yes, that is a serious matter," said the priest. "The best thing you can do is crawl into that woodpile," the priest went on, "and set yourself on fire." The maid did as the priest advised and died in the flames. After Trientje's death the priest always saw a little black dog walking in his garden. Because the animal annoyed him, the clergyman kicked at the dog. "Why do you do that?" asked the animal. "I cooked your meals for so long!" "Hey, Trientje, is that you?" asked the priest. "Yes," answered the dog, "and I am damned for ever." After that day the priest never saw the little dog again.
177573: A woman who had to endure a difficult childbirth vowed that she would go on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel. However, the woman died in childbed. After her death she came to haunt her husband. She took the baby out of the cradle and put it between a chest and a wall. After a while the man decided to make the pilgrimage his wife had once promised himself. When he set off for Scherpenheuvel, he said, "I'll go ahead, follow me." At that the ghost jumped onto his back. If the man had said, "You go ahead, I'll follow you," his wife could not have jumped onto his back.
177576: A man who had just bought new pigs noticed that the animals were behaving strangely. The pigs made a hellish noise and ran into each other in the sty. Moreover, the pigs never ate before midnight. In the end the priests were sent for to overlezen (pray over to lift a spell) the sty. The pigs had been bought from a woman who was suspected of being a witch.
177579:
In Otrange, on the road from Lauw to Wouteringen, a hunchback saw witches dancing. The witches invited the hunchback to dance with them. After the dance the hunchback was freed of his hump. A few days later the man met another hunchback, who asked him how he had lost his hump. The second man decided to go to the witches too. But the second man was given the first man's hump in addition, so that he now had two humps.
Some people going to Otrange saw cats coming out of an alley. In the meadow a witches' circle could be seen.

A hunchback heard the witches at a gathering singing: "Saturday, Sunday, Saturday, Sunday!" When the man added 'Monday' to the song, the witches freed him of his hump.
177600: A drunk man walking from Martenslinde to Berg saw witches dancing in a meadow. The man danced along with them. A while later a second man came to join the dance. When the second man had to sneeze, the first said: "God bless you." The next moment all the witches ran off in the shape of cats. The man was holding not a cup but a bone with urine in it.
177603: In Koninksem a raging black dog with a chain always roamed the street. Everyone was afraid of the animal.
177635: A woman whose husband had been killed in Germany during the war thought she saw the spirit of her late husband appear at night.
177658: Long ago in Sint-Truiden a merchant from Diest was murdered by two boys. After his death the merchant came back to haunt. A song was made about the incident.
177662: At full moon a kitten sat on the wall around the church in Genk. Against his better judgement a man knocked the cat to the ground with a stone. When the man went to sleep that evening, the kitten was already in the barn ahead of him. "Oh my little pussycat, you're going to sleep with us," said the man. The words were barely out of his mouth when the kitten lashed out with her claw at the man who had knocked her off the wall. Just in time the man took his pocketknife and cut the animal's paw. The next moment the cat changed into the maid of the farmer the man was staying with. "If you dare betray me, I'll kill you," threatened the maid. The man never revealed the maid's name.
177664: Whoever threw a stone at a black cat in the evening was chased by a whole pack of cats.
177680: A woman of the V. family had an inflamed arm because of a witch.
177682: Two men, one of whom was a werewolf, worked together. The one man always went outside first, so that he could hide behind a hedge and jump on the other's back as soon as he came out. The werewolf licked the other man and made itself carried.
177683: A woman from Wèzet had just had a baby. Suddenly a hand appeared out of the water pipe and strangled the baby. When another baby was born the following year and the hand again emerged from the water pipe, the father chopped off the hand with an axe. A little later he found that his mother-in-law had lost her hand.
177690: A man woke up at night with a terrible toothache. Because the pain was almost unbearable, the man got up and walked to the little chapel of the saint venerated against toothache. When the man came back from the chapel, he suddenly saw a headless friar floating through the air. Because many people saw that friar, in the end nobody dared to go to the chapel any more.
177709: On the paved road in Hoesselt there was a haunted house.
177715: A man who wanted to cross a bridge was stopped by a cat. The man then gave the animal a blow. The next day the witch went about with a bandage around her head.
177733: A boy was working in the field with a friend. When a man passed by the field, the boy said: "Shall I make that man stand still?" Then the boy stuck his spade in the ground. At that moment the passer-by stood still as if nailed to the ground. As soon as the boy pulled the spade out of the ground, the man could go on again.
177738: The wife of K. from Gessel had a hedge of redcurrants around her house. When the woman saw Marie D. picking currants, she said: "Watch out, because redcurrants give you lice!" When she got home, Marie saw that her shawl was completely full of lice.
177743: A boy visiting his girlfriend pretended to have fallen asleep. Meanwhile all the girls in the room rubbed themselves with witch's grease kept in a pot on the windowsill. Then they said: "Over hedges and hawthorns", and flew to a place overseas, where they danced and leapt. When everyone was gone, the boy also rubbed himself with the witch's grease. But he made a mistake when speaking the magic formula and said "through hedges and hawthorns" instead of "over hedges and hawthorns". When the boy reached the other witches, he was badly injured. His girlfriend said: "How will you get home now? You don't have that power any more!" Luckily one of the witches still had a pot of witch's grease with her. On his return the boy did say "over witches and hawthorns", so he got home safely. But he never wanted to see his girlfriend again.
177761: One night a man was plagued by the maar (nightmare spirit), which gave him a feeling of tightness. From then on the man always put his slippers back to front beside the bed, so that the maar could no longer get at him.
177763: In the old days there lived in Rotem a boy who played the werewolf. He jumped on people's necks and made himself carried. Werewolves were driven by an irresistible urge.
177772: A man going home was followed the whole time by a cat that rubbed against his legs. The man had tried several times to kick the cat, but he could not hit the animal. The cat went with the man until he was home.
177780: A man went threshing with his brother on a farm in Germany. The man was always given apples by an ugly girl from the neighbourhood. Although the other girls said: "You mustn't eat those, because she is a witch", the man had already eaten an apple. At night the men went into the field to pull up sugar beets. Suddenly one of them dropped his dung fork because an ugly cat was sitting on it. Convinced that the cat was the witch, that man threw another dung fork at the animal. Right after that a white and a black rooster walked past.
177788: In Sint-Truiden there lived a witch who went around everywhere asking for potatoes and bread. A girl at whose door the witch had knocked could no longer eat, drink or speak.
177792: A mother walking down the street with her little child met an old woman. After the old woman had laid her hand on the child's little head, it fell ill. That woman must have been a witch.
177793: In the Kempen there once stood an old haunted castle. In the castle of Gestel and in the woods around it strange noises were often heard. The people who lived in the castle believed that the former inhabitants had committed injustice and that their souls could find no rest until they had atoned for their sins. One night the castle's forester was seized by the throat while someone said: "I am the ghost of Gestel and I will claim new victims." That same night there were three knocks on the castle gate. The ghost said: "I will see justice done." The next morning all the inhabitants of the castle were dead.
177812: Pier from the Drevenstraat had been visiting his mother at the Hagedoorn. Pier did not stay away long because his wife Tru was pregnant. When Pier reached his house, he saw a black dog lying in front of the door. Because Pier did not dare to go inside, he walked around for a while. A little later the animal had disappeared.
177813: A boy who was in a relationship with a witch wanted to free his girlfriend. A priest had told him that at midnight he had to walk around the church three times with his girlfriend in his arms. The boy took the cat in his arms and began to walk around. But the cat, which was really his girlfriend, grew heavier and heavier. When the boy had walked around three times, his girlfriend suddenly stood before him saying: "Well Zjo, now I am freed!"
177820: Whoever had not kept a vow had to haunt after his death. Someone else then had to go with the ghost to Scherpenheuvel. Before setting off, the companion had to stand his stick against the wall and force the ghost to go ahead. If this was not done, one had the greatest difficulty reaching one's destination.
177841: People who could not make butter had noticed that cats always came into the stable in the evening. When the people kept watch in the stable one evening, the cats stayed away and butter could be made without trouble. Because a witch from the neighbourhood made their lives miserable, the people had to move in the end anyway.
177860: Two farmhands worked on a farm, one of whom was a werewolf. One evening the farmer and the other farmhand saw the young man crawl into a hollow tree stump and appear a little later in the shape of a werewolf. That farmhand was also going with Lieske K. When the pair came home late one evening, the farmhand said to his girlfriend: "I have to relieve myself behind the bushes. If a beast comes at you in the meantime, throw this red handkerchief at its mouth." A little later a werewolf did indeed appear and tore up the handkerchief. When she got home, the girl found that her boyfriend still had the threads of the handkerchief between his teeth.
177866: A man from Molenbeersel had to carry the werewolf every evening. When one evening the man got the chance to cut the werewolf with a knife, the animal began to bleed and changed into a human.
177867: At the Hoeversnest in Gruitrode a man had called a woman a witch. When the woman threatened to take the man to court, the man had said: "If you dare, you will leave the court in the shape of a cat!" The woman took the man to court, and she did indeed leave the building as a cat.
177868: On the castle avenue of Wideux lay an old felled oak. The count took the oak to the woods on a cart. Strangely enough, the next day the oak was lying in its old place again.
177885: A man regularly visited his girlfriend, who people said was a witch. When the man came home one evening, he got lost, although he knew the way well. At dawn the man saw that he had been standing in front of the gateway of a meadow the whole time. As soon as the sun rose, the witches had no more power.
177893: When Keupke S. was returning from a visit to Fonske in Beringen, he saw a cat sitting in Terlamen. The man struck at the cat with a medlar stick, but he missed. After that the man got lost.
177895: When a werewolf's collar was thrown into the oven, the werewolf was delivered.
177899: Because farmer Harie B. had a lot of misfortune in his stable, people believed that his animals had fallen victim to the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft). The farmer, however, did not believe a word of it. Some time later the farmer's wife secretly went to consult the parish priest, who gave her a blessed relic to hang in the stable. From then on all the animals stayed healthy. Harie B., however, never wanted to believe that the kwade hand had caused the trouble.
177900: When the witch from Piringen lay dying, she passed her power on to Ida from Kerniel. A sick girl was cured by Ida.
177903: A woman's child cried all the time because it had been touched by the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft). Three months later the child had still not recovered. When the parish priest cut open the child's pillow, he found lots of needles bound together in the shape of a devil's tail or a snake whose head was already finished. The priest blessed everything and advised the people to burn the pillow. After that the child was cured.
177926: Some people from Rijkhoven had taken an inheritance to which they had no right. When one of them had died, he came back to haunt with the words: "Keep what you have, I will suffer what I can." That dead person was in hell. When all the goods were finally divided fairly, the ghost was no longer seen.
177927: A woman from Henis had found the wallet of a prior of the American troops. The woman pretended she was going to take the money to the village constable, but in reality she used it to buy three houses. She had no luck, however, because one of those houses was haunted.
177931: In the meadows will-o'-the-wisps often appeared in the evening. They were the little souls of unbaptised children. When people saw will-o'-the-wisps, they began to pray. A little later the lights disappeared because the souls had been released.
177950: A man who had a large pond took his fish to Maastricht by cart. On the way the horse suddenly stood still. The animal was held back by the ghost of a man who had been killed in an accident on that road.
177962:
On Friday 12 May 1900 a fourteen-year-old boy was kicked by a horse, which shattered his ankle. The boy stubbornly kept working all Friday and Saturday. Because it was the fair in Maastricht on Sunday, his mother said to the boy: "You have had to work hard. Go to Sint-Servaas now. Here are five francs to buy a straw hat". When the boy arrived in Maastricht, he was in so much pain that he could hardly walk. So the boy went to the Brusselsestraat to take the tram home. When the boy learned that the tram had left an hour earlier, he cried out in despair: "To the devil, how am I going to get home now!" With the help of a stick the boy hobbled home. It was already half past seven when the boy got home. After he had told his mother what had happened, the woman said: "Put your foot in a bucket of salt. That will take the pain away". But because the pain did not ease, the doctor was called the next morning. The doctor did not touch the foot and said almost at once: "We will have to put leeches on the foot". After the doctor had put three leeches on the foot, the pain eased a little. The next day the pain came back. The doctor put thirty-six leeches on the foot, but none of it helped. Because the foot was inflamed, the doctor cut into the foot with a knife in five places so that the pus could drain. Several months later the foot had still not healed. When the boy was sitting outside one day in September, the brothers of the Passionist order came to collect part of the harvest. One of the brothers looked at the foot and said: "No doctor will be able to cure that. You must go to the priests, but you must not say that I sent you". The boy's father sent for the priests of Rekem. After the priests had prayed for two hours until the sweat dripped from their faces, one of them said: "You will soon feel a great change in your foot. Your family will now pray a novena. The sixty-five students and priests in our monastery will also pray a novena and say a mass every day. When the last mass is said, you will feel an extraordinary change in your foot". On the ninth day a piece of bone came out of the wound. It was a bone with little teeth, like the ones sometimes found in the fields. In all, twenty-eight little bones came out of the foot.
The boy's misfortune was attributed to the wife of a broom maker from the Kempen. The boy's father was chairman and so had to make out the vouchers in exchange for which the poor could get bread. When the father had an ailment in his hand, he had his son make out the vouchers. Although the poor normally got only one loaf a week, that woman from the Kempen came as many as four times. One day the boy said to her: "You are not getting any more bread, because you have had enough already!" At that the woman had answered angrily: "You will regret that!" Exactly one year later the boy had the accident with his foot.
177968: Every time a witch stuck pins into a special little doll, a child in the neighbourhood started to cry. Because the doctor could not help the child, the parents sent for the parish priest. The priest laid a cross of straw on the threshold and fetched some holy water and a palm sprig. Then the priest made a small fire and began to pray. A little later the witch stood at the door. After the priest had removed the straw cross, he forced the witch to come inside. While the priest went on praying, the witch went on working the doll. Then the priest asked the witch to take the doll out of its little box. After the priest had read prayers over the doll and baptised the witch, everything went back to normal.
177979: Some bricklayers from Lummen were walking home together. At a little chapel the men saw a cat sitting on the road. When one of the men kicked at the cat, the animal jumped onto his shoulders.
177984: One night two boys knocked a ghost to the ground. When the boys' father went to look the next day, he found his neighbour lying there on the ground.
177987: In Hoeselt there stood a house that was haunted. A man on his way to Scherpenheuvel saw a black clergyman come out of the house. The ghost went to the churchyard of Bilzen.
177989: A woman coming back late from the fair saw a dog with a red handkerchief in its mouth. A little later the woman met a boy who had the red threads of the handkerchief between his teeth.
177992: On the road to Meeswijk the cowards had to carry the werewolf.
178009: Some people were full of lice after visiting Bet, a fortune-teller from Zonhoven. Those people had to have prayers read over them by the fathers to be rid of the lice.
178013: When Teuke was keeping watch over his potatoes at night, he saw the count of Bovelingen come riding up in his horse-drawn coach. The coach and the horses seemed to be made of fire. From his coach the count called again and again: "Where must I carry it?" For the count was carrying a fiery boundary post on his shoulders. And so it often happened that people from the area saw the count lugging his boundary post around while wailing in despair the whole time. One day, however, an answer to the count's question rang out: "That is where you must put the boundary post." Since then the haunting count has never been seen or heard again. Only through forbidden practices such as moving boundary posts did the count of the castle of Bovelingen manage to gather twelve hundred bunder (an old land measure) together. But such things are always punished.
178016: An old woman suspected of witchcraft could fill a house with rats.
178022: A woman had already had many children, but strangely enough all the children had died shortly after birth. When the woman was pregnant again, a soldier claimed he could save the child's life. During the night of the birth, the soldier saw a cat sneak into the house through the drain hole for the water. Quickly the soldier cut off one of the cat's paws. The next day a woman in the village was going about who had lost an arm. The child born that night survived.
178025: Louike R. told that the late Mrs C. came to haunt the little playhouse.
178026: Farmer Jef A. had his cows milked by a woman who was said to be a witch. Some time later six cows had to be slaughtered because they had gone mad.
178028: The devil had helped build the cathedral of Aken. In return for his help he demanded the soul of the first living creature to enter the finished church. But they cheated the devil by chasing a wolf into the church first. The devil plotted revenge and wanted to bury Aken under a large mountain. While the devil was on his way to Aken with the mountain on his back, he met a little old man, whom he asked how much farther it was. When the little man answered: "That's another two hundred hours' walk", the devil lost heart and dropped the mountain on the spot. The mountain lay not far from Aken, because the little man had fooled the devil.
178034: Muizen L. could make mice. By the church in Bocholt there lived a girl who could also make mice. In the mornings the girl made mice during catechism class. The priest cured the girl of the witchcraft.
178040: In the old days people often talked about the dead who came back to haunt.
178043: A man who had stolen the golden rosary of Our Lady got stuck on the gate. Our Lady had punished the thief for his crime. When the man was found, the court punished him once more.
178065: In Vechmaal there was an alley with thatched houses. Because it was haunted there, the alley was also called the 'spooksteeg' (ghost alley) or the 'hutsteeg'.
178068: In Martenslinde there was a white house that was haunted. Some boys went there one evening to shake apples from the tree. Although the boys had seen and heard apples falling to the ground, afterwards they could not find a single fruit. The next day, however, there were hardly any apples left on the tree.
178086: Werewolves often hid behind a bush or in a wood. When someone came past, the werewolf jumped on that person's back and made itself carried. Drunkards especially had to carry the werewolf. The werewolf often lingered on the road to Heiberich and to Smeermaas, or near "de Eik" and "'t Kruiske". Werewolves could not pass a cross.
178088: A man walking to Meeuwen on a Sunday evening was jumped by the werewolf. The man managed to cut the werewolf in its paws. A werewolf that lost blood took on its human form again. Still the man did not recognise the werewolf. The man told his friends: "Next Sunday we'll know who the werewolf is. I'll go to Mass in Meeuwen, and you must go in Ellikom. If we see a man with a wound on his hand, we'll know who it is."
178093: A mother who had her children fetch milk from Boze Griet always put some salt in the pot. After all, Boze Griet was a witch.
178113: When Harry came into the Kruisstraat, he saw that a witch's house was on fire. As soon as Harry stood in front of the house, it seemed as if he were nailed to the ground. He could not go on until the fire was put out.
178133: A knight who had lost all his money at cards sold his soul to the devil. In exchange for his soul the knight was allowed to live in luxury for seven more years. When playing cards he was never allowed to use clubs, because they looked too much like a cross. Seven years later the knight had to go at midnight to the Geerterbrug (Saint Gertrude's Bridge?) in Heppeneert. Because the knight had burned a candle for Saint Gertrude every evening, he was protected by the saint. "Chase away that old witch behind you!" cried the devil. So the knight was spared by the devil thanks to the help of Saint Gertrude, who sat behind him on his horse.
178134: People who had moved a boundary post during their lives came back after their death to haunt with a boundary post in their arms. Whoever wanted to release such a person had to say: "Put the post back where you took it from."
178139: For seven days in a row after his father's funeral, a young man heard knocking on the wall of his bedroom. He believed it was the spirit of his father, who had not yet found rest. His mother and brothers laughed at him because they did not hear the sound themselves. The young man even took a stone out of the wall to find out what could be causing the knocking. But he found nothing.
178143: A little boy had a little book with him at catechism class with which he could conjure the church full of mice. When the priest had taken the book away, the mice had vanished and the boy could not make any more either.
178147: A woman could make mice. Because her daughters had told others about it, the priest also came to hear of it. The priest called on the woman and asked: "Make some mice for me," but she could no longer do it.
178148: In the old days people had to give alms to the witches who came to the Nonnekerkhof. If they did not, the witch would spit and infest the children with lice.
178168: Anyone ridden by the mare (nightmare spirit) could no longer speak or get up. A man from Kotem who was troubled by the mare asked his brother, who was a priest: "What must I do to be rid of the mare? They say I must put my clogs upside down beside the bed." The priest replied: "Put your clogs however you like!"
178171: When someone wanted to burn a werewolf's collar, the man was at the oven in no time to save his band.
178181: A rural policeman on his rounds saw black cats turn into women and witches fly through the air. The policeman always heard beautiful music.
178188: Every night between twelve and one o'clock a foal ran along the avenue of Damerus castle.
178189: Anny always got lice because of the witch J., who could not get on with her. The parish priest advised Anny to draw a cross on the ground with her foot whenever she met the witch again. Each time Anny did this, the witch fled. She could also no longer come into the house.
178192: The werewolf made its victims carry it and gave off a terrible stench.
178216: The deceased owner of the castle of Voort came to haunt at night with a great deal of noise.
178217:
Before the witches flew off on their broomsticks, they said: "Over hedges and hawthorns to Cologne!" Then they disappeared up the chimney. Witches were bound body and soul to the devil.
A man who wanted to follow the witches on their journey made a mistake when speaking the magic formula and said: "Through hedges and hawthorns to Cologne!" That man got stuck in a hedge on the way.
178219: One day a man walked past the meadow where the school would later be built. The man heard witches making music there. Some time later the man was found above the well, where the witches had hung him.
178227: A man who went about with a little wreath around his neck discovered one day that his wreath was full of lice. The people then said: "You have been touched by the evil hand!"
178243: Stan H. and Louis N. had been visiting some women. Louis stayed talking with the women for a while, while Stan went home ahead. Two young cats leapt in front of Stan's feet, blocking his way. As soon as Louis caught up with Stan, the cats had vanished.
178277: Good people could be tormented by witches for no reason, so that they suddenly stood stock-still in the middle of the street.
178282: N. from Metsteren had a little child who was always ill. In the child's pillow the priests found a hand. Fortunately the thumb was not yet finished, otherwise the child would have died.
178289: A man often went to the monastery in the evening with a friend from the neighbourhood. One evening, however, the friend had a stomach ache, so he could not come along. On the way the man had to crawl through a wide hedge. Only at four in the morning did the man get out of the hedge. That day he had forgotten to sprinkle himself with holy water.
178313: On a farm in Kotem a woman had accidentally let an unlicensed bull escape. They were unable to catch the bull alive, so the farmer suffered a great loss. A woman known as a witch was blamed for the whole incident. When that woman died, the farmer had said: "I will never forgive Trientje for that!" When the farmer was coming back from Valkenburg some time later, he thought he saw the witch in a sunken lane in Catsop with a little basket under her arm. At the moment the witch walked past him, she suddenly vanished. The same thing happened three more times. The farmer had already said "Good evening" twice, but the witch did not answer. The third time the farmer said: "I forgive as I would like to be forgiven." After that the farmer never saw the ghost again. When the man came home, his wife said: "You must stay home tonight, for I have been scared to death today! The whole time I heard a fluttering as if there were pigeons in here." What the farmer and his wife had experienced had happened at exactly the same time.
178320: A woman stroked a child's head. The next day the child was full of lice and fleas. From then on people always kept their children away from the witch.
178321: In Vechmaal lived two sisters and a brother, all three of whom had a hunchback. Because the man was always drunk, one of his sisters often called him a drunkard. One day, between Heks and Vechmaal, the man came upon a troop of cats dancing in a ring. The man had to join the dance. He felt as light as a feather, and when the dance was over, to his great joy, his hunchback was gone. When he came home, he cried: "Look, sisters, what an elegant man I am now!" The sisters were very jealous and one of them said: "You'll get half my fortune if you tell me how you lost your hunchback." The man told his sister the secret, so that the next day she too had lost her hunchback. The other sister, who had always insulted her brother, could now no longer bear her jealousy. She said to her brother: "If you tell me your secret too, drunkard, you'll get my whole fortune. But you mustn't spend it on drink, do you hear!" The man took his sister to the place where the cats danced and told her to join the dance. The sister danced along until at a certain moment she began to cry: "Help, help! I'm getting so heavy that I can't stay upright!" This sister had received the hunchbacks of her brother and her sister as well, so that she now had three. That was her punishment for always having insulted her brother.
178334: A man coming back from Lafelt along a field path was accompanied by a dog. When the man said: "Get lost!", the dog changed into a man. The dog was a werewolf.
178340: A man going to Wijchmaal saw two hares on the way that kept running ahead of him. After a while the man took his gun and shot one of the hares. He could not hit the other hare. Then the man put the dead hare in a sack and went on. A little later the other hare ran past him and said: "Mieke, where are you?" To which the shot hare replied: "I'm already in the sack!" The man was so startled that he promptly dropped his sack and ran away.
178350: A house in Opgrimbie was haunted. At night a white lady came and sat on the horse, which made the animal foam at the mouth.
178352: A man had met a sorcerer in Maastricht who could drive away rats. When the man began reading in the evening in the book of magic he had been given by the sorcerer, his bed was suddenly full of rats. The man had done it wrong.
178353: Four men who had been to the Sint-Andries market in Budel were going back to Hamont along the Kraantjesbeek. A black cat was sitting on the bridge over the brook. One of the men took a stick and knocked the cat into the water. A little further on, a small kitten suddenly walked ahead of them. The man said: "Look what a pretty pussycat!" At once the animal turned around and cried: "If you hadn't spoken to me so sweetly, I would have broken your neck!"
178372: Every evening a shade walked along the Maas calling: "Ferry me over... Ferry me over!" People believed that the man's wife and child had been standing on the other side of the Maas. One day some brave men went to look at the calling ghost. When they came closer, a fierce wind rose and a large shadow flew past. Later the calling was heard much less. It was believed that the man had sunk away into the mud.
178375: Whenever there was a witch nearby, the animals lay in the stable with their legs in the air. After the animals had been overlezen (prayed over to lift a spell) by a clergyman, they behaved normally again.
178385: A man who had to pass a turnstile cross in a meadow at night was surprised that the cross was turning by itself. The man then said: "May God reward you!" A voice answered: "For that reward from God I have had to turn here so long!" It must have been the soul of a dead person.
178401: A man who had gone to visit his girlfriend in Bilzen came home on foot by way of Komveld. The man claimed he had had to carry the werewolf in Komveld. He had not dared to strike the beast.
178406: Near Tongeren there was a farm that was bewitched. One evening some people were given shelter there in the barn. Before the guests went to sleep, the woman made them some soup. During the night, however, the guests in the barn heard a strange noise and a voice saying: "Would you like another spoonful of soup?" To which one of them replied: "I would rather hit you on the head with the spoon!" The woman was a witch.
178418: A drunken man who had fallen asleep in the church saw a priest come in at midnight, go to the altar and put on his vestments. After making the sign of the cross, the priest began the mass. A little later the priest turned around and asked: "Is there anyone who can serve Holy Mass for me?" When the priest had asked for the third time, the drunkard woke up and offered to serve. After the mass the priest said: "I have come here every night for ninety-nine years. Now I am released, but you will die a year from today."
178436: A woman who went around peddling threatened the people who received her badly. Those people could no longer make butter.
178444: A poacher saw a dog and a hare playing together. Because the man wanted to shoot the hare without hitting the dog, he waited for a while. But the game would not stop, and the man went home. Although there was no wind, the leaves of a tree began to blow violently. The man was so frightened that he quickly ran home.
178448: Around ten in the evening a man and his wife were coming back along the Eetseveld from the chapel of Opitter. On the way the woman was followed the whole time by a cat. When after a while they passed a statue of Christ, the cat suddenly vanished. At that moment wonderfully beautiful music rang out.
178458: When a poacher shot at a hare, his gun burst apart. When the man got home, he saw the hare sitting behind the stove.
178463: A cat always came scratching at the drain hole of a house. One day someone chopped off one of the cat's paws. The next day a woman was going about with a broken arm.
178465: A witch who had said by mistake: "Through hawthorn and hedge" arrived at her destination with an injured face.
178470: The kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft) untied the cows and moved the horses to another place in the stable.
178475: Some people going on foot to Spalbeek got lost near a turnstile. After the people had prayed three Our Fathers and three Hail Marys, they found the way again.
178477: A cattle dealer was once murdered in the Biezenbroek in Horpmaal. After his death the man came to haunt there, and people kept hearing: "Help, ow, ow, ow! Help, ow, ow, ow!"
178482: A pigeon fancier from Walshoutem believed that he would have bad luck with his pigeons if a witch from the village came outside while he was basketing them for a race.
178493: Kabotermennekes (gnomes) lived in the Hoverik and on the Fransberg in Ham. There were no dwarfs in Gerhees and Langeven because the weavers there made too much noise.
178501: Whenever hoarse Trijn was nearby, everyone quickly made themselves scarce. For the witch had once touched a little boy and said: "Oh, what a beautiful child you are!" The next day the boy's head was crooked.
178502: A man coming home from work at night met a black dog. The man threw his spade at the dog but failed to hit the animal. The dog walked beside the man the whole time. It was the devil, who came to make it clear to the man that he should do his work during the day.
178507: The werewolf was a man who had wrapped a sheepskin around himself and who made people carry him.
178515: Near the churchyard in Tessenderlo a ghost appeared at night, calling: "Where must I leave this? Where must I leave this?" One day a drunkard answered: "Leave it where you took it from!" After that the ghost was seen no more.
178526: A man coming back from his work in Luik was followed by a black cat that kept running between his legs. When the cat suddenly vanished, the man saw that a woman was standing behind him.
178532: Whenever a farmer had bought a cow, he always put a coin on the threshold of the stable. By stepping over the coin, the animal would drive the evil spirits out of the stable.
178535: In Boyen (Stokkem) there was a haunted house. Stones were always being thrown through the window. The priest came to bless the house and told the occupants all to go to communion on Sunday. When the priest stayed to eat with the people in the evening, a lump of clay suddenly fell from the ceiling into the porridge. In the end the people had to move.
178556: Whenever Metje, the witch of Millen, had been in a stable, the animals were ill the next day. Sometimes the witch also made the children ill.
178558: When Zjang D. walked from Mechelen to Kotem, he saw a man walking ahead of him the whole time. At a bend, Zjang noticed that the man had disappeared. But there was a dog walking on the road.
178559: Every evening a man saw a ghost appear on the road to Maastricht. It was the spirit of a dead person who could find no rest because he had vowed to go on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel. The man decided to go on the pilgrimage for the ghost himself. The priest had advised the man to lay a white handkerchief over his shoulder. When the mass in Scherpenheuvel was over, the man saw that a hand had been burned into the handkerchief.
178576: Anyone who had to pass a turnstile in the evening usually could not get through because a black cat was sitting on it.
178583: A man going to Mass on Sunday morning was suddenly plagued by an unbearable itch. When the man got home, he found two fat lice on his skin. On the way the man had met an old woman who had bumped into him.
178590: There was a song that warned people about witches and ghosts. A woman in a white dress came to complain that no one had yet prayed for her. The people then had to go inside and pray three Our Fathers. Meanwhile the potatoes were stolen.
178594: On the heath there was a haunted spot because a girl had once died there. At midnight bells could be heard ringing underground. Two black cats and one white one would also appear.
178595: A man had visited a friend in the evening. When the man left, the lady of the house said to him: "Make sure you don't get lost!", to which the man had replied: "Even if I walked with my eyes shut, I still wouldn't get lost". As soon as the man had closed the door behind him, strangely enough he could no longer find his bearings. The man strayed so far from the road that someone else had to take him home.
178596: At the R. family's farm the cows could be heard lowing in the stable at night. When they went to look, the animals were sleeping peacefully. It must have been the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft).
178600: When it was very windy, music or the chirping of birds could be heard in a copper beech. When a meeting was held in a café, some men went together to the copper beech. After one of the men had fired his gun into the crown of the tree, a key fell to the ground. The next day an old woman came asking for her house key. She was a witch who had been to the witches' meeting. Such phenomena used to be called the wild hunt.
178612: One evening a man saw a will-o'-the-wisp above the Schijnskuil behind the churchyard of Bocholt. Koob V.E. tried in vain to shoot at the lights with his gun. Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children.
178615: A man from Diepenbeek saw an angel with a cross appear in the sky, followed by two men carrying a gravestone. Some time later cholera broke out at the place where the apparition had appeared.
178621: One day Tuut, a Walloon, was sitting in an inn in Groot-Gelmen. In the inn people said that every evening at half past nine a black dog with a chain around its neck passed by. Because Tuut was a brave man, he went to stand outside around half past nine. When the dog came running up, Tuut was too frightened to utter a word. The beast had run between Tuut's legs.
178625: A witch came to visit people who had bought a fat young pig. "What a beautiful pig!", the witch had said. The pig, however, never had any piglets.
178664: A little boy had to fetch gin for some farmhands. In a sunken lane the boy killed a werewolf with his axe. Some time later the body of the dead farmhand was found.
178665: Witches could not die until they had passed their book of magic on to a child.
178666: A woman whose little son had just died was visited in the morning by a witch from Maastricht, who was out with a cart. At that a friend of the mother shouted angrily: "Now that you have killed him, you come to look!"
178668: 'Pie de klak' was known as a poor beggar. After Pie drowned himself in a pond, the suicide had to come back to haunt. Gold coins had been found all through the cap of 'Pie de klak'.
178669: A young man was seeing a girl who was suspected of being a witch. People warned the boy: "You had better be careful with that girl. If you visit her on three Fridays in a row, you will know whether she really is a witch." The boy followed the advice and from then on visited his girlfriend only on Fridays. When the girl asked whether he could not come on another day, the boy said he had no time then. On the third Friday the girl turned out not to be at home. Because he did not want to go home straight away, the boy spent the evening with his girlfriend's neighbours. When the boy wanted to leave for home, the girl called out: "Come to me now; I am back here now." But the boy knew enough, and he never wanted to see the girl again.
178690: A family from Gelinden could not make butter whenever the witch Bet had visited. When they sprinkled some salt in the milk, it went a little better.
178700: The silk lady came out of the brook in her rustling dress and walked along with passers-by as far as an alley, where she went off towards the Jeker.
178702: At the fair in Rijkhoven two girls were approached by a boy who asked if they wanted to go for a walk. One of the girls accepted, so her friend stayed at the fair alone. When the boy was on the way with the girl, he said: "You go to that café for a bit. I have to relieve myself." The girl answered: "No, I'll wait for you here." The boy gave the girl a handkerchief in case she was attacked by a dog. Further on the girl did indeed meet a dog. The girl threw the handkerchief at its mouth and then decided to wait for the young man in the café after all. When the young man came into the café, he said: "What happened to you? You look so frightened!", to which the girl replied: "I saw a nasty dog. The beast tore the handkerchief to shreds. It was you, because the threads are still hanging between your teeth!"
178721: A man mowing corn was hindered the whole time by a big black cat running between his legs. When the man came home in the evening, he thought he saw a scarf lying on the ground. When the man went to pick up the scarf, it turned out to be the cat, blocking his way. That cat may well have been a witch.
178723: In Piringen, six black witch cats came to sing and dance in a meadow in the evening.
178724: After his death a man came back to haunt with a boundary post in his arms. When a little old woman met the ghost and said: "In God's name, put it back where you took it from!", the man was released.
178759: In the meadow by the alley next to the church stood a cherry tree. In it sat a ghost that made a terrifying noise.
178781: A farmer had a farmhand who always went out in the evening. One evening, however, the farmer saw the farmhand sit down on a tree stump, crawl through a leather ring and then turn into a werewolf. The next day the farmer threw the boy's collar into the fire. At once the farmhand came rushing up to pull his collar out of the oven. When the collar had burnt up completely, the farmhand said in relief: "Now I am delivered, now I am free."
178790:
In Mal there once lived a man who had to go about as a werewolf.
Since Napoleon gave the order to shoot all werewolves, the beasts have died out. In Mal a werewolf was once beaten to death with a dung fork.
If you could make a werewolf bleed, you could recognise him.
178792: A werewolf roamed the Pitsesteeg in Rutten. If you could make a werewolf bleed, he was freed.
178808: One evening the count's forester had to keep watch at Haspershoven. When Frans saw a mewing cat sitting on the road, he loaded his gun with two cartridges. The next moment some thousand cats were dancing and leaping on the road. Those cats were witches holding a meeting. "Now I must get through," said Frans, "or I'll shoot you dead." At that the cats moved aside to let Frans pass.
178857: A little boy who had not been baptised could make mice by blowing on a little heap of sand.
178865: In the evening people always heard someone calling by the Maas: "Ferry me over! Ferry me over!"
178879: People who went home late in the evening had to carry the werewolf.
178882: A boy out walking with his girlfriend said to the girl: "You go on, because I have to relieve myself. If you meet a dog, just throw this handkerchief." A little later a dog did indeed appear, and it tore the handkerchief to shreds. When the boy came back, the girl told him how frightened she had been. To her great dismay the girl found that her boyfriend still had the threads of the handkerchief between his teeth.
178897: Under the bridge on the road to Gotem lived a ghost that overturned the wagons of passing farmers. When the wagon had been righted with great effort, the ghost would often overturn it again. Eventually a friar was sent for to drive the ghost away. When the friar had read prayers over the ghost, he wanted to make it come out from under the bridge. The ghost then cried: "You can do nothing to me. I know you once stole a cabbage from a garden somewhere." "That is true," answered the priest, "but I did leave half a franc in that spot." At that moment the priest gained power over the ghost, which was banished to a tree.
178898: Betje was talking to a man. After the man had been given a pat on the shoulder, he was completely covered in lice. Betje was a witch.
178901: A farmer who wanted to buy two pigs ignored a witch who predicted that the animals would die. But the next day the pigs were dead.
178911: If people saw a black cat sitting on the road, they believed it was a witch and kicked at the animal. People going on pilgrimage who met a black cat on the way began to sweat heavily and could go no further.
178915: A boy had to go and buy tomatoes for his father. In the shop stood a woman who was said to be a witch. The woman said admiringly: "What beautiful tomatoes!" When the boy got home, all his tomatoes were rotten.
178918: A farmer's wife who spent the whole day churning butter attracted the attention of her neighbours. The other women asked her: "How is it that you have so much milk?", to which the farmer's wife replied: "That is very simple. I never run short of milk." The farmer's wife took a little key from behind the door, threw it under the churn and then said: "Now a spoonful from every house." At that the churn was completely full of milk again. The women tried to take the little key from the farmer's wife, but they did not get it.
178922: At night a black cat often roamed about, getting under the feet of passers-by. As soon as the cat leapt at someone, it vanished.
178930: A bewitched child died after eight days.
178933: A miller's boy often had to go and help a farmer in the evening when a foal was being born. By the church path the boy, to his great fright, saw a beguine who put her hand on the hedge and blew warm steam into his face.
178943: On a farm in Gruitrode the windows and doors always flew open. A beggar who came to spend the night in the barn saw someone come in at twelve o'clock, knock a stone out of the wall and begin counting gold coins. The ghost counted the gold coins three times and then said: "Half for the church and half for whoever releases me." As soon as the ghost had disappeared, the beggar came out. He took the money out of the wall, gave half to the church and kept the other half for himself. From that night on the farm was no longer haunted.
178945: Trui S. was an unmarried woman who received many male visitors. When a man knocked one evening, Trui refused to let him in. As soon as Trui came back into the room, however, a big black dog sat there growling. After Trui made the sign of the cross, a loud thunderclap sounded and there was a strong stench of sulphur. The dog was gone. After that incident Trui went to the priest and mended her ways.
178951: Two brave men who saw a white lady appear in the churchyard ran away in fear.
178953: A man shot with his gun at a hare sitting in his garden. Although the hare was not dead, the man had hit the animal. The next day the woman next door lay wounded in bed.
178964: A man claimed that a witch lived in a street in Vlijtingen. Since then that little street was called the 'Heksenstraatje' (Witches' Lane). A woman who went sewing at people's homes in the evening walked home along the Vossteeg. When the woman rested for a moment at a turnstile, a big cat suddenly came and sat beside her. The woman stroked the cat and said: "I still have so far to go and it is dark. I'll be going now." The cat answered: "I'll go with you. Then you needn't be afraid." When the woman reached her house, the cat said: "Now you needn't be afraid any more. Now you are here and nobody can do anything to you. If you come again next week, I will wait for you again and go with you." The woman went inside and saw through the window that the cat had changed into a witch wearing an apron. The witch took the apron out from under her broom and flew away.
178972: A farmer was full of lice after a witch had patted him on the shoulder.
178975: Fien Van G. made sure that the witch Johanna G. could not come near her newborn child. One day, however, Johanna had got the chance after all to stroke the child's head. That same evening the child developed a fever. If the parish priest had not been sent for quickly, the child would certainly have died.
178985: One day a witch said to a woman: "Let your daughter Liesje come to me, because I have a beautiful hat for her". The woman, however, did not want her daughter to accept anything from a witch. So the witch brought the hat herself. Two days later Liesje fell seriously ill.
179003: When the poachers in the Dennendreef tried to shoot a hare, their guns did not work. For those hares were the deceased inhabitants of the castle, who came back to haunt in the form of an animal.
179042: On a farm in Heythuyzen all the animals became restless at midnight, so that they were completely drenched in sweat. The owner of the farm, which the farmer rented, was a witch.
179061: A boy who went walking with his girlfriend 'in de Buts' said on the way: "Go on ahead. I have to relieve myself." The boy gave his girlfriend a handkerchief and said: "If you meet a big dog, throw this handkerchief at its mouth. Then the dog won't be able to hurt you." Further on the girl did indeed meet a dog. She threw the red handkerchief at the animal. When her boyfriend came back, the girl saw that he still had the threads of the handkerchief between his teeth. The girl never wanted to see the boy again.
179071: A man learned from a fortune-teller that his mother-in-law was infesting his children with lice.
179099: A banished spirit lived under the bridge of Bocholt. Every hundred years the parish priests of Gerdingen, Bocholt and Beek came to the bridge with altar boys to read prayers for half an hour. In this way the spirit was banished again each time for ninety-nine years.
179105: A girl who went to herd the cows could conjure her clogs full of mice, although there were no mice anywhere nearby. That is why people believed the girl was a witch.
179135:
Long ago part of Zoutleeuw perished as punishment for the unchristian way of life of its inhabitants.
One day a girl found a stick by the water with a red silk thread tied to it. When the girl began pulling the thread, there seemed to be no end to it. Finally a bell rose out of the water. But the girl was so startled that she cried out: "Jesus, Mary!" At that the bell fell back into the water.
179139: A soldier on guard duty saw the light in a house come on every time a cat had jumped in through the window. When the cat left again, the light went out. That cat was a witch.
179144: When Jang N. went to the shop, he met a woman on the way and stayed talking with her for a while. After he had been to the shop, Jang met a dog as big as a horse. Jang threw his handkerchief at the animal's mouth and ran away. When Jang met the same woman again a few days later, he found that she still had the threads of the handkerchief between her teeth.
179150: A brave soldier spent the night in a haunted castle. After the man had drunk some wine, he began to bake cakes over the fire. Suddenly, however, a bone fell out of the chimney. "Is the game starting already?" said the soldier, and he took the bone out of the pan and threw it in a corner. The same thing happened several more times, until a complete skeleton lay in the corner. While the soldier was eating, the skeleton came towards him. "Watch out, little man," said the soldier, "or I'll smash your ribs with this bottle!" The ghost gestured to the man to go somewhere with it. The man let the ghost go first and followed it to a place where a stone with a ring lay on the ground. The ghost asked the man to lift the stone, but the man said: "No, lift that stone yourself!" After the ghost had lifted the stone, three pots of money could be seen. "One pot is for you, one for the poor and one for the church," said the ghost.
179153: Werewolves could change into all kinds of animals, except a sheep and a donkey. For Our Lord was the Lamb of God and He rode on a donkey.
179163: A farmer had a maid who went spinning somewhere every evening to earn a little extra. One day the farmer warned his maid: "If I were you, I wouldn't go spinning at that place tonight. If you do go, you must take a red handkerchief. If a dog comes at you, you must throw the handkerchief at the beast." That evening the maid did indeed meet a big black dog. The next day the farmer asked her whether she had seen anything, and the maid answered: "Yes, I saw a werewolf, and I threw the red handkerchief at the beast." The farmer then said: "Yes, that werewolf was me," and he pulled the red threads from his teeth, saying: "If you dare betray me, you're done for." The maid never told anyone what had happened to her.
179176: At Driek P.'s place a black cat always sat in the henhouse. Because Driek found that annoying, one day he hit the cat with a club. A few days later Driek heard that Fien M. had a dislocated arm. Fien claimed she had fallen down the stairs, but Driek had his own thoughts about it.
179179: During the French Revolution the house of Jan V.B. in Hechtel was 'zwart goed' (church property seized and sold off). A clergyman named F. had been murdered in that house at the time. After his death Friessen came to haunt with a book under his arm. The animals always became very restless then.
179224: Three sisters were going to Mass on Christmas night when one of them saw a ghost sitting by the ditch of Groemmes.
179240: The daughter of a witch from Paal went to the ball against her mother's wishes. The girl fell down dead while she was dancing.
179246: The alvermannetjes (little elf-men) came to people's homes at night to polish everything. The dwarfs disappeared once it was decided to ring the bells every evening; the dwarfs could not bear that noise.
179256: A farmer whose stable was bewitched lost thirteen calves in the space of one year. The farmer had already asked several parish priests for help, but none of them dared to bless the stable. In the end the fathers of Weert helped the farmer.
179264: A man who had gone to fetch milk met an old woman on the way. The woman warned the man that the jug was full and that he should take care not to spill. When the man poured the milk out of the jug at home, he found a fat toad at the bottom of the jug. The man was convinced that the witch had conjured the toad into the jug.
179267: On a winter Thursday evening a man went by moonlight to visit his girlfriend. On the way the man passed a house where the dead Jan K. came back.
179282: In Wijer, soldiers passing through stayed a few days to rest. The people asked one of the soldiers whether he would keep watch by the churchyard at night, because a black dog had often been seen running past and then disappearing behind the church. Against all warnings the soldier shouted: "Let the damn thing come, I'll bloody well stab it to death!" When the dog came running from the direction of the castle that evening, the priest opened his window and called to the soldier: "Leave the beast alone; it does no one any harm!" But the soldier would not listen and walked towards the dog, cursing. The next day the soldier was found; he had not been bitten, but he was as black as soot. Afterwards a friar banished the dog for ninety-nine years into a hole in the hedge through which it always used to crawl.
179285: A woman who was knitting socks was visited by a witch. When the witch left, the knitting was suddenly full of lice.
179306: A man was jumped by the werewolf between Lanklaar and Dilsen. The man managed to wound the werewolf with a knife. The so-called werewolf was someone who jumped on people to steal their money.
179311: In the churchyard of Munsterbilzen noise and music could always be heard, although there was nothing to be seen.
179330: A man decided to commit suicide by jumping off a bridge. But when he had almost reached the water, he repented. After his death people believed the man was damned and that there was little point in having masses said for him. Then suddenly, during the consecration, a white dove walked across the altar. At that moment people realised that the man was not damned.
179342: In Gellik a man who had committed suicide came back to haunt. The ghost was ablaze. When a clergyman came to banish the ghost, the suicide's son had to walk in front to lead his father's spirit. If the son dared to look back, he would be killed.
179356: A man who was taking his cow to the field met a witch on the way, who said: "Watch out that the cow doesn't swell up." A while later the witch's prediction came true.
179375: A woman from Kotem swore up and down that she was not afraid of the werewolf. When the woman walked to Hal one evening, she met the werewolf by the Maas dike. The woman gave the werewolf such a thrashing that the beast was still lying beside the dike in the morning. The woman had found out that the werewolf was a man from Kotem who had thrown a skin over himself.
179377: During the French Revolution some soldiers had left money for safekeeping with the uncles of Baanbartje. Because those men later refused to return the money, they had to come back to haunt after their death. At midnight the glasses rattled and the farmhands were lifted out of their beds.
179388: The baker's wife had a bad reputation. Whenever she was talking to someone, she always nudged that person with her fist. One day the witch bewitched someone with a swelling under the arm.
179394: A witch laid her hand on the head of a child who was playing. A little later the child was full of lice.
179398: Fonske Van E. boasted that he could take any bird from its nest, no matter what kind of tree the nest was hidden in. Trien B. claimed that she knew a nest Fons could not reach. She pointed to a nest in a low willow. Laughing, Fonske climbed into the tree, but he slipped when he had almost reached the nest. Fons had broken his left leg.
179401: Some people sitting by the fire saw a kitten come in and said: "What a pretty kitten!" The animal replied: "If you hadn't spoken so nicely, I would have broken your neck".
179417: A black woman always came to haunt a farm at night.
179420: Two men coming back from the fair in Meeuwen knocked at the house of two young women. But no one opened. Suddenly a bumblebee flew against the window. One of the men said: "Knock again now; now they'll be home!" They were witches.
179421: Jef's little child died because it was bewitched.
179435: After a witch had stroked a child's leg, the child's leg was paralysed.
179436: A man whose vegetables were all being eaten by hares stood guard with his gun. When the man saw three hares and wanted to shoot the animals, his gun would not work. Someone had advised the man to hold the gun by the barrel and point it at the hares. After the man had done so, he hit one of the hares. The man went to look and recognised his wife and his two daughters.
179438: One evening a man was walking past the churchyard in Gelinden. There he heard music so wonderfully beautiful that he went back to listen to it again a few days later. The music seemed to be made by angels. Each time the man left, he saw a light in the field.
179439: In Donk there stood a gallows where people were hanged. That place was haunted.
179448: A man cycling to the fair met a witch on the way. The witch looked the man straight in the eyes, so that he rode into the ditch.
179450: Witches often came to dance around a tree in B.'s meadow. When they did, wonderfully beautiful music rang out. One day Tans, a woman who lived next to the meadow, feared the witches would pick all the apples from the tree. But Tans needed the apples, because she had to bake a tart for Sunday. So Tans went to the apple tree in the meadow. Before she even reached the tree, she suddenly got a hard slap in the face, so that her cheek swelled right up. The next day Tans met a woman who asked: "Well Tans, what's wrong with your face?", to which Tans replied: "Surely you can see my cheek is swollen!" The woman then said: "You'd better stay indoors in the evening instead of wandering around outside!"
179463: A man who had gone to play cards in the evening saw a ghost jumping in front of him the whole way. "Even if you are the devil," said the man, "I'm not getting out of the way any more." When the man made the sign of the cross, the strange apparition suddenly vanished.
179481: Witches could move about much faster than other people. A pregnant woman was advised by her neighbour never to talk to a witch until the child was born.
179487: Mele M. bewitched her own children.
179506: A small group of people were going to Klein Mal at night between midnight and one o'clock when they suddenly saw a white lady walking with a pram. She walked past the group without saying a word.
179507: When a man drove past a witch's house with his horse and cart, the witch said: "I'll still be home before you!" The man got lost and was still not home the next morning.
179510: The castle of Wijer was so badly haunted that the horses sometimes became very restless. When the animals had been tied up, a little later they would be standing back to front in the stable.
179521: A boy who went walking with his girlfriend said to the girl on the way: "I have to relieve myself. You go on to the café. If you meet some beast or other, throw this handkerchief at its mouth." The girl did as she had been advised. When the boy came into the café a while later, he still had the bits of the handkerchief between his teeth. If the girl had not thrown the handkerchief at the wolf, she would have been dead.
179533: A beggar woman from Rukkelingen touched a little child in a house. Because of this the child had a twisted hand for the rest of its life.
179546: In Tongeren there was a little child that cried all the time. The child had been struck by the evil hand of Bökemänneke, who had stuck the boy's pillow full of pins. After the child's parents laid a cross in front of their door, Bökemänneke dropped dead.
179556: When a witch had stroked a child's head, the child became disabled. Either the child became paralysed, or its head was crooked. The harm could only be undone by the witch herself.
179558: Because P. owned a lot of zwart goed (church property seized and sold off), he came to haunt his castle after his death. The ghost was banished under a stone with the help of chains. Flames appeared on that stone.
179575: In Herstappe there used to be a castle that was haunted.
179580: Beneath the castle of Hocht ran a brook that flowed into the canal. At night a ghost always appeared by that brook, crying: "Ai!"
179585: In Sint Ool there once stood a church in honour of Saint Odilia. Because the church sank into the ground, the bell is heard ringing twelve times from under the ground every year on Christmas night. Whoever tries to go to that place on Christmas night never gets there.
179612: Because Driek's sheep could not lamb, the man sent for the parish priest. After the priest had said prayers over the sheep three times, the witch was seen sitting in the pen. After that the sheep could lamb.
179620: When a plague epidemic raged in Beek, many cows died on all the farms. On one farm they were also plagued by the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft). The farmers had to pull the cart themselves because the horses refused. When the haystack (1) was opened, a little doll fell to the ground. Although everyone had seen the doll fall, there was nothing to be seen on the ground any more. After the parish priest and the chaplain had said prayers over the farm to drive out the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft), no more strange things happened.
179640: A farmer known for his exceptional fruit harvest had never had such bad fruit as in the year his harvest was bewitched.
179674: A dead man who had hidden money somewhere during his life had to haunt until his money was found.
179682: In Stevoort there was always a black dog that blocked everyone's way. That was the devil.
179688: A woman going to Elderen was followed by the devil in the shape of a cat. When the woman quickened her pace, the cat walked faster too. Only when the woman entered her house did the animal disappear.
